title: Identification of dynamic regimes in continuous time under treatment-dependent observation is unresolved
text: GMT-02 Unverifiable High priority Emerging Tractability 2/5

title: Identification of dynamic regimes in continuous time under treatment-dependent observation is unresolved
text:
Statement
Treatments, outcomes and clinical observations occur asynchronously and are recorded at times determined by the care process. Discretizing that onto a grid can reverse the temporal ordering of a treatment and an outcome falling in the same interval, merge several events into one, and define an estimand that exists only relative to the chosen interval. Identification and efficient estimation for dynamic interventions in continuous time under counting-process filtrations and irregular monitoring have been established. They do not yet settle the case an emulation on routine data actually faces: a visit process that depends on treatment, combined with effects that occur inside an interval. A continuous-time emulation must define the treatment, covariate, visit, censoring and outcome processes relative to a filtration and impose assumptions linking latent histories to the observed visit process, and most applied emulations still discretize without an identification result tied to the grid they chose.

title: Identification of dynamic regimes in continuous time under treatment-dependent observation is unresolved
text:
Why it is open
In continuous time the treatment, visit and outcome processes are counting processes whose intensities depend on one another, so sequential exchangeability has to be stated with respect to filtrations rather than a fixed sequence of covariate vectors, and the resulting conditions are stronger and harder to interpret. Grid-refinement analyses can reveal sensitivity to discretization and cannot establish identification, so the diagnostic available to applied work does not answer the question it raises. There is also no natural sample-size asymptotics, because information about an intensity comes from event counts rather than from patients.

title: Identification of dynamic regimes in continuous time under treatment-dependent observation is unresolved
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Tankpinou Zoumenou H, et al. Time Partitioning in Target Trial Emulation. arXiv 2026
Treats the partition of time as a modeling choice with consequences rather than as a convention, which is the entry point to the continuous-time question.


Robins JM, Hernán MA, Brumback B. Marginal structural models and causal inference in epidemiology. Epidemiology 2000;11(5):550-560
The discrete-time identification result that continuous-time work has to generalize, stated with sequential exchangeability, positivity and consistency.


Goldstein BA, Bhavsar NA, Phelan M, Pencina MJ. How and when informative visit processes can bias inference when using electronic health records data for clinical research. J Am Med Inform Assoc 2019
Establishes that the visit process in electronic health records is informative, which is the condition that makes the continuous-time problem hard rather than merely technical.

title: Identification of dynamic regimes in continuous time under treatment-dependent observation is unresolved
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend the existing continuous-time identification results to treatment-dependent visiting with within-interval effects, and state which conditions a standard electronic health record violates. Combine marked point-process models, continuous-time structural nested models and neural differential equations, constraining the learned components to the nuisance functions identification actually requires, so flexibility sits where it cannot manufacture a contrast. Report invariance across nested grids as a routine diagnostic while stating what it does and does not establish.

title: Identification of dynamic regimes in continuous time under treatment-dependent observation is unresolved
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source said. “Treatments, outcomes and clinical observations occur asynchronously and are recorded at times determined by the care process. Almost every applied g-method assumes a prespecified discrete grid, and discretization can reverse temporal ordering between a treatment and an outcome that fell in the same interval, merge multiple events into one, or define an estimand that exists only relative to the chosen interval. General identification results for dynamic regimes under irregular observation, treatment-dependent visiting and within-interval effects remain limited, so the applied analyst working in continuous time has a modeling apparatus without an identification theorem to sit under it.”
What was wrong with it. Continuous-time identification and efficient estimation for dynamic interventions under counting-process filtrations and irregular monitoring have been established, so the claim that the analyst has no identification theorem was wrong. What those results do not yet settle is the treatment-dependent informative visit process together with within-interval effects, as an apparatus an applied analyst can use by default.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported-with-caveat): The entry says general implementable identification results for dynamic regimes under irregular, treatment-dependent observation remain limited. Estimation in that setting is further along than the entry allows. Continuous-time marginal structural model weights built from a marked point process have been constructed and applied where visit times are irregular and informative and treatment history carries duration and dose. G-computation and doubly robust standardization for continuous-time data have been compared with inverse probability weighting. What has not been supplied is the general identification theorem the entry asks for, stated in filtration terms and covering within-interval effects, so the theoretical half of the claim stands while the estimation half is weaker than written. grok dissented (overstated): The claim that continuous-time dynamic-regime identification under irregular, process-driven observation is essentially without an identification theorem is stronger than the literature allows. Rytgaard, Gerds, and van der Laan (Annals of Statistics 2022) give a continuous-time counting-process TMLE for intervention-specific means when treatment, covariates, and outcomes occur at subject-specific times; intensities track monitoring; dynamic regimes on treatment assigned are defined with visit times kept as they naturally occur; and identification is via continuous-time g-computation under sequential exchangeability and positivity on the product-integral likelihood. Røysland, Ryalen, Nygård, and Didelez (JRSS-B 2025; arXiv:2202.02311) supply nonparametric graphical identification criteria for marginal effects of interventions on treatment-process intensities in continuous-time survival and event-history models, including structural conditions on censoring beyond classical independent censoring. Earlier continuous-time MSM and structural nested model work (Røysland; Ryalen et al. on prostate cancer) already stated filtration-based sequential exchangeability. What remains open, and why this is only partial: applied g-methods still default to discrete grids (Tankpinou et al. arXiv:2603.15924 still treats time partitioning as a consequential modeling choice); Rytgaard’s main identification path intervenes on treatment decisions while leaving the visit intensity natural, so full dynamic control of a treatment-dependent informative visit process plus within-interval effects is not a closed applied recipe for EHR; software for continuous-time LTMLE is not yet a routine TTE default. Proposal papers that add unmeasured confounding (for example arXiv:2604.00544) are not resolutions. Identification theory exists; the residual gap is completeness for treatment-dependent observation, within-interval estimands, and routine practice.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The entry says general implementable identification results for dynamic regimes under irregular, treatment-dependent observation remain limited. Estimation in that setting is further along than the entry allows. Continuous-time marginal structural model weights built from a marked point process have been constructed and applied where visit times are irregular and informative and treatment history carries duration and dose. G-computation and doubly robust standardization for continuous-time data have been compared with inverse probability weighting. What has not been supplied is the general identification theorem the entry asks for, stated in filtration terms and covering within-interval effects, so the theoretical half of the claim stands while the estimation half is weaker than written. Cites 10.1002/sim.70102: Constructs continuous-time marginal structural model weights via a marked point process precisely because primary-care visit times are irregular and informative and treatment history has duration and dose.. Cites 10.1177/09622802211047345: Compares continuous-time g-computation and doubly robust standardization against IPW, which is the estimator comparison the entry proposes as future work..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The difficult open component is identification and estimation under explicitly defined full-data and observation-process assumptions, not a wholesale absence of continuous-time identification theory. Treatment-dependent visiting does not by itself destroy identification; the analyst must specify assumptions linking the latent longitudinal process to what is observed, together with treatment, observation and censoring positivity. If clinically relevant covariate history between visits is unobserved and no coarsening or observation model is imposed, the regime effect is generally not identified. Filtration-based exchangeability is different from, but not automatically strictly stronger than, every discrete-time formulation. Coarsening can erase or impose an incorrect ordering, although it does not mechanically reverse ordering in every shared interval. The claim that there is no natural sample-size asymptotics is false: independent patients provide a standard n-to-infinity sequence, and counting-process estimators use martingale asymptotics, with information also affected by event counts and follow-up. Grid refinement is a sensitivity analysis, not an identification test; instability does not localize a unique failure, and stability cannot validate exchangeability or the observation model.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

partially-solved / overstated. The claim that continuous-time dynamic-regime identification under irregular, process-driven observation is essentially without an identification theorem is stronger than the literature allows. Rytgaard, Gerds, and van der Laan (Annals of Statistics 2022) give a continuous-time counting-process TMLE for intervention-specific means when treatment, covariates, and outcomes occur at subject-specific times; intensities track monitoring; dynamic regimes on treatment assigned are defined with visit times kept as they naturally occur; and identification is via continuous-time g-computation under sequential exchangeability and positivity on the product-integral likelihood. Røysland, Ryalen, Nygård, and Didelez (JRSS-B 2025; arXiv:2202.02311) supply nonparametric graphical identification criteria for marginal effects of interventions on treatment-process intensities in continuous-time survival and event-history models, including structural conditions on censoring beyond classical independent censoring. Earlier continuous-time MSM and structural nested model work (Røysland; Ryalen et al. on prostate cancer) already stated filtration-based sequential exchangeability. What remains open, and why this is only partial: applied g-methods still default to discrete grids (Tankpinou et al. arXiv:2603.15924 still treats time partitioning as a consequential modeling choice); Rytgaard’s main identification path intervenes on treatment decisions while leaving the visit intensity natural, so full dynamic control of a treatment-dependent informative visit process plus within-interval effects is not a closed applied recipe for EHR; software for continuous-time LTMLE is not yet a routine TTE default. Proposal papers that add unmeasured confounding (for example arXiv:2604.00544) are not resolutions. Identification theory exists; the residual gap is completeness for treatment-dependent observation, within-interval estimands, and routine practice. Cites 10.1214/21-AOS2114: Provides continuous-time counting-process identification (g-computation on product integrals) and efficient TMLE for time-varying and dynamic treatment interventions when monitoring times are subject-specific; models monitoring intensities and covers dynamic regimes on treatment assigned with natural visit schedules.. Cites 10.1093/jrsssb/qkae056: States nonparametric graphical identification criteria for marginal effects of interventions on continuous-time treatment-process intensities using local independence / counting-process graphs, including structural conditions on censoring; directly supplies the filtration-style identification theorem the agenda says is missing.. Cites arxiv:2603.15924: Does not close identification; documents that discrete time partitioning remains a consequential open modeling choice in applied TTE, which supports residual openness after continuous-time theory..

glm

open / supported. The claim is coherent and proportionate. It says general identification results ‘remain limited’ rather than asserting they do not exist, which correctly frames this as a gap in current theory rather than a structural impossibility. The reason given for openness is substantive: in continuous time, exchangeability must be stated over filtrations, conditions are strictly stronger than discrete counterparts, and event-count-based asymptotics do not scale the way patient-count asymptotics do. These are genuine theoretical obstacles, not mere inconveniences. The scope is appropriately narrow—dynamic regimes under irregular observation and treatment-dependent visiting—rather than overgeneralizing to all continuous-time causal inference.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2/4) → R7:counter-and-support-both-present(support=1/counter=1)

title: A hazard ratio is reported where the estimand was a weighted per-protocol effect among the grace-period compatible
text: EST-03 Unverifiable Very high priority Established Tractability 5/5

title: A hazard ratio is reported where the estimand was a weighted per-protocol effect among the grace-period compatible
text:
Statement
Hazard ratios, odds ratios and model coefficients are routinely presented without naming the intervention, the population, the time horizon or the strategy for each intercurrent event. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement both require that objectives, estimands and sensitivity analyses be aligned, and applied reporting has not caught up. A correctly executed clone-censor-weight analysis with a grace period estimates a marginal contrast between prespecified strategies in the baseline eligible population, and where the artificial censoring enforces adherence that contrast is per-protocol. A bare hazard ratio discloses none of this: not the intervention, not the strategies, not the population, not the horizon, not the handling of intercurrent events. It is therefore read as an intention-to-treat contrast by default, and nothing in the presentation contradicts that reading.

title: A hazard ratio is reported where the estimand was a weighted per-protocol effect among the grace-period compatible
text:
Why it is open
The hazard ratio survives every methodological improvement beneath it, so better estimation does not change what gets read. Stating the estimand precisely requires naming the strategies and the horizon, and the horizon is a commitment most analyses would rather not defend. The estimand vocabulary and the absolute-risk alternatives both exist and are used in methodological work; what does not exist is a requirement that an applied emulation use them, so the practice is a reporting convention rather than a capability gap.

title: A hazard ratio is reported where the estimand was a weighted per-protocol effect among the grace-period compatible
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




ICH E9(R1) addendum on estimands and sensitivity analysis in clinical trials
Defines the estimand attributes, population, treatment, endpoint, intercurrent-event strategy and summary measure, that an emulation report would have to fill in.


Hansford HJ, Cashin AG, Jones MD, et al. Transparent reporting of observational studies emulating a target trial: the TARGET statement. JAMA 2025
A 21-item checklist requiring the target protocol and its emulation to be reported, aimed at transparency rather than at risk-of-bias certification.


Maringe C, Benitez Majano S, Exarchakou A, et al. Reflection on modern methods: trial emulation in the presence of immortal-time bias. Int J Epidemiol 2020;49(5):1719-1729
Makes explicit that clone-censor-weight analyses target per-protocol-type contrasts rather than baseline intention-to-treat effects.

title: A hazard ratio is reported where the estimand was a weighted per-protocol effect among the grace-period compatible
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Require a one-sentence estimand statement naming the intervention, the strategies, the population, the horizon and the intercurrent-event handling, positioned before any effect measure. Report absolute risks, risk differences and restricted mean outcomes at clinically meaningful horizons, with the hazard ratio as a supplement rather than the headline. Include a timeline diagram showing treatment paths and censoring rules, since a cloning-and-censoring design is easier to draw than to describe.

title: A hazard ratio is reported where the estimand was a weighted per-protocol effect among the grace-period compatible
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source said. “Hazard ratios, odds ratios and model coefficients are routinely presented without naming the intervention, the population, the time horizon or the strategy for each intercurrent event. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement both require that objectives, estimands and sensitivity analyses be aligned, and applied reporting has not caught up. The concrete failure is specific rather than general: a reader sees a hazard ratio and infers an intention-to-treat contrast, while the analysis in fact estimated a per-protocol effect, weighted for informative censoring, among the subset of patients whose observed treatment stayed compatible with a strategy during a grace period. Those are different quantities in different populations and nothing in the presentation distinguishes them.”
What was wrong with it. The population named in the original was wrong, and the error matters because it is the error the entry accuses others of. Correct clone-censor weighting does not target the subset whose treatment stayed compatible: the weights reweight uncensored clone-time observations to stand for the artificially censored ones, so the contrast is in the baseline eligible population under the specified strategies. Where censoring enforces adherence the contrast is per-protocol, and the population is still the eligible one.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): The estimand vocabulary is arriving in the emulation literature: a 2026 Trials paper applies a hypothetical strategy to the intercurrent event of non-adherence using the parametric g-formula, which is the ICH E9(R1) discipline executed inside a longitudinal analysis, and a 2026 Journal of Epidemiology paper argues explicitly for going beyond the hazard ratio when censoring, confounding and competing events are present. The entry’s claim is about what published reports lead with rather than what is possible, and no reporting requirement in the corpus mandates a one-sentence estimand statement or absolute-risk reporting. The presence of these papers means the entry should not imply the vocabulary is missing. codex dissented (overstated): The reporting concern is valid, but the stated population is wrong. Correct clone-censor weighting does not target only patients whose observed treatment remained compatible. It reweights uncensored clone-time observations to represent artificially censored observations, thereby targeting the baseline eligible population under the specified strategies, subject to exchangeability and positivity. A bare hazard ratio identifies neither an intention-to-treat nor a per-protocol strategy and may lack a causal interpretation altogether. TARGET supplies much of the reporting solution; the residual issue is adoption rather than an unresolved estimand method.

The problem is framed as a presentation/practice failure after standards already exist: a reader sees a bare hazard ratio and infers an intention-to-treat contrast, while the analysis estimated a censoring-weighted per-protocol effect among grace-period–compatible (often cloned) patients. Maringe et al. (IJE 2020; 10.1093/ije/dyaa057), already cited, already makes the CCW estimand type explicit; that formalizes the distinction and does not change what applied papers headline. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement (JAMA 2025; 10.1001/jama.2025.13350) require aligned objectives, estimands, and sensitivity analyses; TARGET item structure places target-trial protocol/estimand items (6a–g) beside emulation mapping (7a–g), and item 13 asks for effect estimates with precision including both absolute and relative measures when applicable. Official TARGET resources confirm that scope and provide protocol table and flow-diagram templates. That is real progress on the reporting-standard side and is the caveat on support: the claim is still true about practice, but “standards are missing” would be overstated after TARGET 2025. What remains open is exactly what the report names: applied reporting has not caught up; the HR remains a familiar default that survives estimator upgrades; and nothing forces a one-sentence estimand that names intervention, population induced by cloning/censoring, horizon, and intercurrent-event strategy before the first effect measure. open / supported. The statement is well-scoped and proportionate. It accurately describes the specific mismatch between the reported effect measure (a hazard ratio) and the actual estimand (a per-protocol effect among the grace-period compatible) in clone-censor-weight analyses. The reasons for it being open (cultural inertia of the hazard ratio, difficulty of clinically describing the cloned population, and reluctance to commit to a time horizon for absolute measures) are practical and structural barriers that genuinely support the problem being open.

title: Emulation assumes no interference, and cloning individuals can produce joint strategies nobody could implement
text: EST-01 Confirmed open High priority Emerging Tractability 2/5

title: Emulation assumes no interference, and cloning individuals can produce joint strategies nobody could implement
text:
Statement
One person’s treatment can change another’s outcome through infection, provider behavior, household exposure or a shared resource constraint. Target trial emulation as normally practiced invokes no interference, and under that assumption an individual-level protocol is coherent. Identifying a direct or spillover effect requires more than adding the interference literature alongside it: the emulation has to specify a feasible joint or stochastic treatment policy, the exposure mapping or potential-outcome indexing that defines what each unit is exposed to, and joint support for that exposure. Individual clone-censor rules do not identify those effects, because a set of individually compatible strategies need not correspond to any allocation a cluster could receive. Eligibility, assignment and positivity all become cluster- or network-dependent quantities, and the TARGET reporting guideline offers no cluster-trial extension.

title: Emulation assumes no interference, and cloning individuals can produce joint strategies nobody could implement
text:
Why it is open
There is no canonical exposure mapping: own treatment plus treated-neighbor proportion is one choice among many, and different choices give different and equally valid effects, so the estimand has to be argued rather than derived. Positivity must hold for the joint neighborhood exposure, which is far stronger than individual positivity and typically fails in observed networks. Networks are measured with error, and contagion, homophily and spillover are only weakly separable even when the network is known exactly.

title: Emulation assumes no interference, and cloning individuals can produce joint strategies nobody could implement
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Papadogeorgou G, Mealli F, Zigler CM. Causal inference with interfering units for cluster and population level treatment allocation programs. Biometrics 2019;75(3):778-787
Defines direct and spillover effects for cluster and population-level allocation, one of the frameworks that would have to be joined to the emulation protocol.


TARGET reporting guideline, official resources
The reporting standard for emulations, whose stated scope is parallel-group, individually randomized target trials, so cluster designs fall outside it.

title: Emulation assumes no interference, and cloning individuals can produce joint strategies nobody could implement
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Define network target trials in which the exposure mapping and the feasible joint or stochastic policy are protocol components rather than analysis conveniences, and state the positivity condition for the joint exposure explicitly. Develop cluster-level clone-censor-weighting, in which compatibility is judged for the allocation a cluster could receive rather than for each individual, alongside network targeted learning and agent-based g-computation. Test sensitivity to network mismeasurement by deleting edges at known rates, since a method correct on a perfect network and silent on a noisy one is not usable.

title: Emulation assumes no interference, and cloning individuals can produce joint strategies nobody could implement
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “One person’s treatment can change another’s outcome through infection, provider behavior, household exposure or a shared resource constraint. Target trial emulation as normally practiced assumes this does not happen. Methods under partial interference define direct and spillover effects and are well developed in their own literature, but they are rarely joined to emulation, and the join is not cosmetic: eligibility, assignment and positivity all become cluster- or network-dependent quantities. Cloning individuals independently, which is the standard device for grace periods, can assign a set of clones a joint strategy that no cluster could actually receive, so the artificial censoring is then censoring on an impossible world. The TARGET reporting guideline currently offers no cluster-trial extension.”
What was wrong with it. The account of cloning was imprecise. Cloning creates strategy-specific copies of an individual; it does not itself assign a realized joint allocation to a cluster. The failure is in intervention definition, consistency and joint positivity when individual strategies are read as a joint allocation, not in the artificial censoring operating on an impossible world.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Nothing in the corpus defines a network target trial with an explicit exposure mapping, cluster-level clone-censor-weighting, or a positivity condition stated for joint neighborhood exposure. The interference literature is present in the corpus only through its own methodological line, and the multi-site and distributed-analysis papers address data governance rather than interference. The claim that individual cloning can assign clones a joint strategy no cluster could receive is a structural argument the entry makes rather than one the corpus states, and it follows from the definitions.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The interference problem is technically real, but the cloning account is imprecise. Cloning creates strategy-specific copies of each individual; it does not itself assign a realized cluster jointly. Identification fails when those individual strategies are interpreted as an infeasible or unsupported joint allocation. That is a failure of intervention definition, consistency, or structural joint positivity, not artificial censoring on an impossible world. Eligibility also need not always be cluster-dependent. The status vote concerns this technical problem and does not rely on claims about rarity or current TARGET scope.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. Inverted-prior search did not find a solution that joins partial-interference identification to target-trial emulation in a way that closes the gaps named in the statement. Papadogeorgou et al. (2019), already cited, supplies cluster/population allocation estimands under interference; it does not supply an emulation protocol, joint-neighborhood positivity diagnostics, or clone-censor rules that keep cluster strategies feasible. Buchanan et al. (Stat Med 2022; 10.1002/sim.9427) is the closest prior art: it defines a target-trial protocol for disseminated (spillover) effects of MOUD within provider-based clusters using routinely collected data, so the “rarely joined” claim should be read as rare rather than never. That paper is an application and estimation sketch under partial interference for a specific provider-cluster exposure mapping; it does not invent cluster-level clone-censor-weighting, does not resolve non-canonical exposure mappings, and does not evaluate network mismeasurement. Lu et al. (arXiv 2604.12900, 2026) propose emulating stepped-wedge cluster randomized trials for staggered policy adoption; that covers group-level policy emulation and mentions spillovers as a shared design concern, not individual-treatment cloning that assigns impossible joint strategies. Official TARGET resources (target-guideline.org, retrieved 2026) still scope the checklist to parallel-group, individually randomized target trials, list “Emulation of a cluster target trial” as a possible future extension, and state that no extensions are currently in development, which confirms rather than repairs the reporting gap. Searches across AJE/Epidemiology/IJE/EJE/JCE/PDS/Stat Med/Biometrics, arXiv stat.ME, medRxiv, and package activity (TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, gfoRmulaICE, lmtp, ltmle, CICI, WeightIt) found no merged software that implements network/cluster-compatible clone-censor-weighting or network TMLE for TTE. Contagion/homophily/spillover non-separability and joint-neighborhood positivity remain structural; sensitivity to edge deletion is proposed in the agenda and was not found as a standard TTE tool. Vote open: prior art proposes joins in narrow settings; none solves exposure-mapping canonicity, joint positivity, network error, or cluster-compatible cloning as stated.

glm

open / supported. The statement is internally consistent and proportionate. It correctly identifies that standard target trial emulation assumes no interference, and that joining interference methods to emulation is non-trivial because eligibility, assignment, and positivity become cluster-dependent. The reasons given for it being open (lack of canonical exposure mapping, stronger positivity requirements for joint exposures, and network measurement error) are valid structural methodological challenges that entail the problem is open. It does not assert an impossibility, but rather a current gap in joined practice.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-overstatement(n=1/4):codex

title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
text: ELG-01 Partially addressed High priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
text:
Statement
Trial eligibility is assessed at a screening visit; a database records what a clinician happened to order. Restricting an emulation to patients with complete eligibility information can bias it when observation of the criterion depends on determinants of treatment or outcome that the recorded history does not adequately control, which is the ordinary case when testing tracks severity and access. Weighting and missing-data methods for unrecorded eligibility now exist in more than one paper. The harder version remains: eligibility is latent rather than merely missing, since an absent creatinine value is consistent both with a patient who would have failed the criterion and with one who was never tested. When true eligibility among unobserved records is missing not at random, the effect in the truly eligible population is not identified from the main data alone and requires either additional identifying assumptions or external information.

title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
text:
Why it is open
Missing-at-random conditional on the recorded history is not credible here, because the recording decision is a clinical judgment informed by the same severity that predicts the outcome. The external information that would identify the effect is a validation source in which the criterion was assessed for everyone, and such sources are rare, rarely representative, and rarely transportable to the analysis population. Imputing the underlying measurement and imputing the eligibility indicator need different models, so an implementation has to choose which object it is modeling and defend that choice, and applied work seldom states which it did.

title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Benz L, et al. Adjusting for selection bias due to missing eligibility criteria in emulated target trials. Am J Epidemiol 2025
Develops weighting for missing eligibility information in emulated trials.


Missingness in eligibility criteria for target trial emulation in EHR with survival outcomes. Stat Med 2026
A second direct treatment of the problem, for survival outcomes in record data.


Wang, et al. An operational target trial emulation framework for causal inference using electronic health records. npj Digit Med 2026
Sets out how each protocol component, eligibility included, is realized against record-level data and where the realization is partial.

title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Model true eligibility and its observation jointly, anchoring the measurement model on validation records where the criterion was assessed for everyone. Compare multiple imputation, inverse-probability-of-eligibility weighting, doubly robust selection correction and partial-identification bounds on the same data, stating for each whether the model is of the measurement or of the eligibility indicator, since they are not interchangeable even when they target the same estimand. Report the eligible population under each approach alongside the effect, because a method that changes who is in the trial has changed the estimand.

title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Trial eligibility is assessed at a screening visit; a database records what a clinician happened to order. Restricting an emulation to patients with complete eligibility information therefore selects on laboratory testing, clinical documentation and specialist access, which differ systematically from the excluded patients. Weighting methods for missing eligibility have recently been developed and the literature remains small. The harder version of the problem is that eligibility is latent rather than merely missing: an absent creatinine value is consistent both with a patient who would have failed the criterion and with one who was never tested, and the missingness itself may depend on treatment anticipation or on the impending outcome.”
What was wrong with it. Systematic differences between the included and the excluded do not by themselves establish bias for a specified estimand; the bias arises when observation of the criterion depends on determinants of treatment or outcome that the recorded history does not control. The literature is also larger than one paper. The entry’s claim that imputing the value and imputing eligibility have not been separated was too strong: they require different models, and coherent implementations of either can target the same causal estimand.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): The entry says the literature on missing eligibility is small. It is small and it is larger than the one paper the entry cites. A 2026 Statistics in Medicine paper treats missingness in eligibility criteria for target trial emulation in electronic health records with survival outcomes, alongside the 2025 American Journal of Epidemiology weighting paper the entry already carries. The harder claim, that eligibility is latent rather than missing and that an absent value is consistent with both a failed criterion and an untested patient, is not addressed by either and stands. codex dissented (overstated): Restricting analysis to records with observed eligibility can cause selection bias, but systematic differences between included and excluded patients do not alone establish bias for a specified causal estimand. Identification depends on conditional exchangeability for the observation or selection process and adequate observed support. When true eligibility is missing not at random, the effect among truly eligible patients is generally not identified from the main data alone. However, assessing the criterion for everyone in a validation source is sufficient, not necessary. A probability validation subsample, auxiliary-variable restrictions, explicit parametric assumptions, sensitivity analysis, or partial-identification methods can also inform the problem. If eligibility is a deterministic threshold of an underlying measurement, imputing that measurement and deriving eligibility can target the same population as directly imputing eligibility. Changing imputed membership across draws represents missing-data uncertainty and does not automatically change the estimand. Existing weighting work addresses an important identified-assumption case, while the unrestricted latent-eligibility problem remains open.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. The entry says the literature on missing eligibility is small. It is small and it is larger than the one paper the entry cites. A 2026 Statistics in Medicine paper treats missingness in eligibility criteria for target trial emulation in electronic health records with survival outcomes, alongside the 2025 American Journal of Epidemiology weighting paper the entry already carries. The harder claim, that eligibility is latent rather than missing and that an absent value is consistent with both a failed criterion and an untested patient, is not addressed by either and stands. Cites 10.1002/sim.70500: A second and more recent direct treatment of the problem, which the entry’s claim of a very small literature should acknowledge.. Cites 10.1093/aje/kwae471: The weighting approach the entry already cites..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. Restricting analysis to records with observed eligibility can cause selection bias, but systematic differences between included and excluded patients do not alone establish bias for a specified causal estimand. Identification depends on conditional exchangeability for the observation or selection process and adequate observed support. When true eligibility is missing not at random, the effect among truly eligible patients is generally not identified from the main data alone. However, assessing the criterion for everyone in a validation source is sufficient, not necessary. A probability validation subsample, auxiliary-variable restrictions, explicit parametric assumptions, sensitivity analysis, or partial-identification methods can also inform the problem. If eligibility is a deterministic threshold of an underlying measurement, imputing that measurement and deriving eligibility can target the same population as directly imputing eligibility. Changing imputed membership across draws represents missing-data uncertainty and does not automatically change the estimand. Existing weighting work addresses an important identified-assumption case, while the unrestricted latent-eligibility problem remains open. Cites doi:10.1093/aje/kwae471: Provides a weighting approach for selection arising from missing eligibility information under identifying assumptions; it does not nonparametrically identify unrestricted missing-not-at-random latent eligibility..

Grok 4.5, recency lens

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Inverted prior: treat missing-eligibility selection as already handled, then check what exists. Three direct method papers (not one) address the complete-case selection problem under explicit missingness models. Tompsett et al. (2023) formalize bias from missing eligibility in a point-treatment TTE, show patterns under MAR and MNAR, and evaluate multiple imputation of the eligibility-defining variables plus MNAR sensitivity shifts; they state that MNAR imputation remains exploratory because the sensitivity parameters are not identified from the data alone. Benz et al. (2025; also arXiv:2406.16830), which the entry cites as the first direct treatment, develops inverse-probability-of-ascertainment weights for sequential TTE with time-to-event endpoints under an eligibility-MAR assumption (ascertainment independent of true eligibility given non-eligibility covariates and treatment), evaluates them in plasmode EHR simulations, and applies them to a Kaiser Permanente bariatric-surgery cohort; accompanying research code is on GitHub (lbenz730/missing_eligibility_tte), not a production CRAN/Python package. Shen et al. (2026, Stat Med) compares complete-case analysis with three multiple-imputation strategies for eligibility-defining variables in EHR survival TTEs and reports that flexible MI often reduces bias when missingness is high. Wang et al. (2026) map eligibility realization in EHR data and cite Tompsett and Benz as the handling literature; they do not add a new estimator. What remains open, and matches the entry’s harder claim, is latent eligibility: an absent lab is consistent with never-tested versus would-have-failed, with recording driven by the same severity that predicts treatment and outcome (MNAR not cured by MAR IPW or standard MI). No paper retrieved jointly models true eligibility and its observation process anchored to a validation source where the criterion was assessed for everyone; no head-to-head of MI, IPW, doubly robust selection correction, and partial-identification bounds on the same TTE data with reporting of the implied eligible population under each method was found. Package search (TrialEmulation, WeightIt missing-covariate handling, gfoRmula, lmtp, ltmle, zEpid, causallib) shows no shipped inverse-probability-of-eligibility-ascertainment or joint latent-eligibility measurement model. 2025–2026 guidance (TARGET, FDA RWE/ECT, EMA registry, NICE RWE) does not resolve identification of latent eligibility. Partial solve covers MAR complete-case selection; the title problem (unrecorded criterion indistinguishable from met criterion) stays open. Cites 10.1093/aje/kwac202: Partial: identifies and simulates selection bias from missing eligibility in TTE; evaluates MI of eligibility-defining variables and MNAR sensitivity imputation for recovering the eligible-population ACE under stated MAR/MNAR mechanisms (point treatment, continuous/binary outcome setting).. Cites 10.1093/aje/kwae471: Partial: IPW framework for selection due to incomplete eligibility ascertainment in sequential TTE with time-to-event endpoints under an eligibility-MAR assumption; simulation evaluation and real EHR application. Does not identify effects when missingness depends on latent eligibility itself.. Cites 10.1002/sim.70500: Partial: compares complete-case analysis versus three MI strategies for eligibility-defining variables in EHR survival TTEs; empirical guidance on when flexible MI reduces bias under high missingness. Still imputes recorded values rather than separating latent eligibility from observation.. Cites arxiv:2406.16830: Same as Benz 2025 AJE; states the eligibility-MAR assumption used by the weights and makes clear that standard complete-case analysis targets a different estimand (eligible complete cases, not all eligible)..

glm

open / supported. The claim is internally consistent and pitched at the right level of generality. It correctly identifies that restricting to complete cases selects on healthcare utilization, and that the latent eligibility problem is distinct from simple missingness. The stated reasons for the problem being open (MAR is not credible, validation sources are rare, and imputing a value is different from imputing eligibility) logically entail that the problem remains open. The claim does not assert an impossibility but rather a current methodological gap and a structural difficulty in distinguishing latent states from missing measurements.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2/4) → R9:substantiated-overstatement(n=1/4):codex

title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
text: DTA-02 Partially addressed High priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
text:
Statement
Distributed health data improve power and support transportability, and patient-level sharing is often prohibited, which is why federated emulation has been developed to the point of pooled-equivalent estimation for time-to-event outcomes. The statistical machinery for combining site estimates is not the hard part. Sites differ in coding systems, treatment availability, confounding structure and time resolution, so one executable protocol can define materially different eligibility, exposure and outcome at each site, and pooling then averages several different questions. Aggregation cannot detect that: heterogeneity between site estimates is produced equally by real effect modification and by mapping failure. Local validation and aggregate diagnostics shared without patient records can flag some of it, and no current practice requires either, or requires the target population and pooling weights to be stated.

title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
text:
Why it is open
The incompatibility is semantic rather than statistical: two sites can both return well-estimated, internally valid effects for populations the protocol did not intend to distinguish, and no summary of the estimates reveals it. The diagnostics that would reveal it need either patient-level data, which federation exists to keep local, or agreement in advance on what to compute and share, which is a governance problem rather than a methods problem. Heterogeneity statistics cannot separate the two causes because both produce between-site variance.

title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Li, et al. Federated target trial emulation using distributed observational data for treatment effect estimation. npj Digit Med 2025
Demonstrates that distributed effect estimation for an emulated trial is feasible without pooling patient-level data.


Manke-Reimers M, et al. When, why and how are estimated effects transported between populations? A scoping review. Eur J Epidemiol 2025
Reviews transport practice, which is the framework needed to say what a multi-site average is an estimate of.

title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
text:
Probable solution or research direction
State the target population and the pooling weights in the protocol so the pooled quantity is a transported effect for a named population rather than an unweighted average of whatever the sites produced. Share sufficient statistics, influence curves and aggregate balance measures, which is enough to diagnose incompatibility without moving patient records, and adopt the multi-site conduct principles now being codified for distributed analysis. Gate aggregation behind site-level component validation, so a site that fails contributes to the report and not to the estimate.

title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Distributed health data improve power and support transportability, and patient-level sharing is often prohibited, which is why federated emulation has been proposed and demonstrated for distributed effect estimation. The statistical machinery for combining site estimates is not the hard part. The hard part is that sites differ in coding systems, treatment availability, confounding structure and time resolution, so the same executable protocol can define materially different eligibility, exposure and outcome at each site. Averaging the resulting estimates produces a number whose estimand is the average of several different questions, and nothing in the aggregation step detects that.”
What was wrong with it. Nothing in the aggregation step detects it, which the entry stated correctly, but local validation and privacy-preserving aggregate diagnostics can flag some incompatibilities without centralizing records, so the situation is not undiagnosable. Federated estimation for emulated trials has also advanced past the feasibility demonstration the entry cites.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Federated emulation has advanced past the feasibility demonstration the entry cites. POLARIS supplies a one-shot likelihood approach for federated emulation with time-to-event outcomes that claims pooled-equivalent estimates, and a 2026 JAMIA paper sets out ten principles for high-quality multi-site studies using privacy-preserving distributed algorithms, which is directly the site-validation discipline the entry asks for. The entry’s specific claim, that averaging site estimates can conceal that sites emulated different trials and that nothing in the aggregation detects it, is not answered by either: both improve the statistics of pooling rather than detecting semantic incompatibility. Cites 10.21203/rs.3.rs-9613167/v1: Provides pooled-equivalent federated estimation for emulated trials with survival outcomes, well past feasibility.. Cites 10.1093/jamia/ocag119: Codifies multi-site conduct including site-level validation, which is the gate the entry proposes..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The central warning is correct: operational differences can make site-specific estimates contrasts for different populations, interventions, outcomes, or follow-up regimes. A pooled result is still mathematically an average under specified weights, but it is not automatically an effect for a scientifically meaningful target population. Heterogeneity statistics cannot identify whether variation reflects effect modification, sampling error, positivity problems, or semantic mapping failure. The impossibility claim is too strong, however. Patient-level centralization is not required for all relevant diagnostics; sites can return cohort attrition, prevalence, support, balance, event rates, code-set provenance, and other privacy-preserving summaries after local validation. Conversely, sufficient statistics, influence curves, and balance summaries are not enough to establish semantic equivalence. A transport model also cannot repair incorrectly defined variables and requires explicit target-population and effect-modification assumptions. The open problem is reliable semantic validation and governance under federation, not the complete absence of diagnostics.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. The report’s own cited work, Li et al. (FL-TTE, 2025), demonstrates that distributed effect estimation for an emulated trial is feasible without pooling patient-level data. That is estimation machinery, not a solution to semantic incompatibility: sites can still implement different eligibility, exposure, or outcome mappings under the same executable protocol, and averaging site estimates does not detect that. Manke-Reimers et al. (2025) is a scoping review of transportability practice; it clarifies when a multi-site average needs an explicit transport model, but does not supply site-level diagnostics that separate mapping failure from true effect modification using only the aggregates federation is allowed to share. Recent federated causal-inference methods (for example Khellaf, Bellet, and Josse on propensity-score aggregation across sites; LATTE one-shot federated TTE showcased at OHDSI 2025) again address statistical pooling and privacy-preserving nuisance estimation, not semantic trial equivalence. Queries across AJE/Epidemiology/IJE/EJE/PDS/SiM, arXiv stat.ME, medRxiv, and package ecosystems (TrialEmulation, lmtp, ltmle, WeightIt, MatchIt, gfoRmula) did not surface a released method that gates secure aggregation behind site-level trial-component validation or that diagnoses coding-system and phenotype discordance from sufficient statistics and aggregate balance alone. Heterogeneity statistics remain confounded between real effect modification and mapping failure, exactly as the problem states. Status remains open as stated.

glm

open / supported. The claim is coherent and pitched at the right level of generality. It accurately identifies that the core difficulty in federated emulation is semantic incompatibility rather than statistical combination. The reasons given for it being open (diagnostics require patient-level data that federation restricts, and heterogeneity statistics conflate mapping failure with effect modification) directly support the claim that the problem remains open.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1/4) → R9:substantiated-overstatement(n=1/4):codex

title: Convergence of treatment in the comparator arm attenuates the observational intention-to-treat analogue with follow-up length
text: CNF-01 Overstated High priority Established Tractability 4/5

title: Convergence of treatment in the comparator arm attenuates the observational intention-to-treat analogue with follow-up length
text:
Statement
The observational analogue of an intention-to-treat effect contrasts assigning initiation now against not initiating now, and in that contrast the comparator group does not stay untreated: patients frequently initiate later. Reduced separation between the treatment histories can move the estimated effect at longer horizons, in a direction and by an amount that depend on the treatment-effect dynamics, the switching mechanism, the competing events and the effect scale. This is a feature of the estimand rather than a bias to be removed, and it occurs in randomized trials too. What emulations do not do is report it: the cumulative incidence of initiation in each arm over follow-up is rarely published, so a reader cannot judge how far the contrasted strategies stayed distinct, and a null result at a long horizon cannot be read against the convergence that actually occurred.

title: Convergence of treatment in the comparator arm attenuates the observational intention-to-treat analogue with follow-up length
text:
Why it is open
The convergence is a property of the strategy contrast, so it cannot be adjusted away without changing to a per-protocol estimand that carries its own assumptions, and methods for that exist. The reporting gap is what remains, and it persists because the trajectories are an extra analysis that weakens no result and strengthens none. There is also no convention for choosing the horizon at which an open-ended no-initiation arm is still a meaningful comparator, and the rate of convergence depends on the health system and calendar period rather than on anything intrinsic to the treatment.

title: Convergence of treatment in the comparator arm attenuates the observational intention-to-treat analogue with follow-up length
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Hernán MA, Robins JM. Using big data to emulate a target trial when a randomized trial is not available. Am J Epidemiol 2016;183(8):758-764
Defines the observational analogues of the intention-to-treat and per-protocol effects and states what each requires.


Cain LE, Robins JM, Lanoy E, Logan R, Costagliola D, Hernán MA. Using observational data to emulate a randomized trial of dynamic treatment-switching strategies. Int J Epidemiol 2016;45(6):2038-2049
Handles later initiation and switching explicitly through dynamic strategies, which is the design response to convergence.


Statistical methods to adjust for treatment switching in real-world clinical studies: a scoping review and decision framework. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2025
Catalogs the available methods for treatment switching and supplies a framework for choosing among them, which is the body of work the entry originally overlooked.


Caution in handling switchers in pharmacoepidemiologic studies estimating treatment effects. Am J Epidemiol 2026
Sets out the analytic hazards specific to switchers in effect estimation.


Addressing treatment switching in the ALTA-1L trial with g-methods: exploring the impact of model specification. BMC Med Res Methodol 2024
Applies g-methods to switching and examines how sensitive the result is to specification.

title: Convergence of treatment in the comparator arm attenuates the observational intention-to-treat analogue with follow-up length
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Report the cumulative incidence of initiation in both arms over follow-up alongside the effect estimate, so the separation between strategies is visible rather than assumed. Prefer contrasts that name the later initiation explicitly, such as initiate now versus initiate on a stated clinical trigger, over an open-ended no-initiation arm the data will not sustain, and use the existing switching methods when the per-protocol question is the one being asked. Quantify by simulation how a given convergence rate moves the estimate at each horizon under different effect dynamics, so the reader has something to read a null against.

title: Convergence of treatment in the comparator arm attenuates the observational intention-to-treat analogue with follow-up length
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Methods for handling treatment switching exist and have been reviewed; emulations do not conventionally report initiation trajectories in both arms, so a reader cannot judge how far the contrasted strategies remained distinct over follow-up.
The source said. “The observational analogue of an intention-to-treat effect contrasts assigning initiation now against not initiating now. Two things then happen that do not happen in a randomized trial. Assignment is confounded, so the contrast requires baseline adjustment to mean anything. And the comparator group does not stay untreated: patients assigned to no initiation now frequently initiate later, so with longer follow-up the two strategies converge and the estimated effect attenuates toward the null for reasons that have nothing to do with the treatment’s efficacy. The attenuation is a function of the follow-up horizon and of local prescribing behavior, and it is rarely reported as such, so an emulation with long follow-up and a null result cannot be distinguished from one where the treatment does not work.”
What was wrong with it. Two errors. Crossover into the comparator arm happens in randomized trials as well, so it is not something that happens only in an emulation. And attenuation toward the null is not guaranteed: the direction and size depend on the treatment-effect dynamics, the switching mechanism, competing events and the effect scale, so a convergence rate alone does not determine an attenuation factor. Methods for handling treatment switching also exist and have been reviewed, which the entry did not acknowledge.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The entry treats comparator convergence as an unhandled feature of the observational intention-to-treat analogue. Treatment switching is a well-developed area with its own methods and its own scoping review. A 2025 Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics scoping review catalogs statistical methods to adjust for treatment switching in real-world studies and offers a decision framework for choosing among them. A 2026 American Journal of Epidemiology paper warns specifically about how switchers are handled in pharmacoepidemiologic effect estimation, and a 2024 BMC Medical Research Methodology paper applies g-methods to switching in the ALTA-1L trial. The entry’s implicit claim that the analyst has no options is wrong. What survives is narrower and still real: reporting the cumulative incidence of initiation in both arms is not conventional, so a reader cannot see how far the strategies stayed distinct, and no convention exists for choosing the horizon at which the contrast remains meaningful. Cites 10.1002/cpt.70013: Catalogs the available methods and supplies a framework for choosing among them, which contradicts the entry’s implication that convergence cannot be addressed.. Cites 10.1093/aje/kwaf044: Addresses the specific analytic hazard of switchers in effect estimation.. Cites 10.1186/s12874-024-02437-6: Applies g-methods to switching and examines the sensitivity of the result to specification..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. The valid core is that a baseline-assignment, treatment-policy analogue permits subsequent initiation, so increasing crossover can reduce exposure separation and may dilute the assignment effect. This is part of that estimand, not confounding bias to be adjusted away. However, crossover also occurs in randomized trials, so it is not uniquely observational. Convergence of current treatment status does not imply convergence of cumulative exposure histories, and attenuation toward the null with longer follow-up is not guaranteed: its direction and magnitude depend on treatment timing, effect dynamics, switching mechanisms, competing events, and the effect scale. A convergence rate alone therefore cannot determine an attenuation factor. Nor does a null estimate become categorically indistinguishable from biological inefficacy; treatment trajectories, alternative sustained or dynamic-strategy estimands, and assumption-based analyses can clarify interpretation, although they cannot identify a decomposition without additional assumptions. Existing target-trial and dynamic-strategy methods substantially address the design problem; context-specific horizon selection and adequate trajectory reporting remain unresolved practice issues. High severity is justified only when the reported estimand is mischaracterized or exposure separation is inadequate for the intended decision. Cites 10.1093/aje/kwv254: Provides the distinction between observational analogues of intention-to-treat and per-protocol effects and the corresponding design and adjustment requirements.. Cites 10.1093/ije/dyv295: Shows that later initiation and switching can be specified explicitly as dynamic strategies rather than treated as an unaddressable convergence problem..

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. Under an inverted prior, the open components of CNF-01 were treated as likely already closed by method, reporting guidance, or software; searches do not support that closure. The phenomenon itself is long recognized: observational assignment-to-initiate contrasts are confounded at baseline, and later initiation in the non-initiator arm dilutes the observational intention-to-treat (ITT) analogue as follow-up lengthens. Hernán and Hernández-Díaz (Clin Trials 2012; doi:10.1177/1740774511420743) document ITT dilution under nonadherence and argue for careful per-protocol (PP) work in comparative effectiveness. Hernán and Robins (Am J Epidemiol 2016; doi:10.1093/aje/kwv254), already cited, define observational ITT versus PP analogues and what each requires; they do not supply a reporting convention that forces cumulative initiation trajectories in both arms beside the effect estimate, nor a rule for a still-meaningful horizon. Cain et al. (Int J Epidemiol 2016; doi:10.1093/ije/dyv295), also already cited, is the main design response: name later initiation via dynamic strategies rather than an open-ended never-initiate arm. That changes the estimand; it does not identify or “debias” the attenuated ITT contrast under realistic crossover. Recent restatements keep the issue open rather than solved. Terman (Neurology 2025; doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000214269) states that the ITT effect is typically attenuated to the degree patients switch after assignment, with a statin initiator versus noninitiator example where PP was stronger than ITT. Molero-Calafell et al. (J Clin Epidemiol 2024) restate that ITT can dilute effects when adherence differs. TARGET (Cashin et al., JAMA 2025; doi:10.1001/jama.2025.13350) is the strongest recent reporting push: it requires naming the causal contrast (assignment versus adherence), mapping strategies to data, and reporting sensitivity to design and analysis choices. From published summaries of the 21-item checklist, it does not mandate cumulative incidence of treatment initiation in both arms over follow-up as a standard diagnostic of strategy convergence, and it does not establish a horizon convention for when an initiate-now versus not-now contrast remains interpretable. STaRT-RWE, HARPER, NICE RWE framework, FDA RWE/data-source materials, ENCePP, and ICH E9(R1) improve estimand language and protocol structure generally; none close the specific CNF-01 gap that a long-horizon null observational ITT cannot be read against the convergence that produced it. Package checks (TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, lmtp, ltmle, WeightIt, MatchIt, cobalt, riskRegression, adjustedCurves, zEpid, causallib) show outcome cumulative-incidence tools and ITT/PP estimation, not a merged standard for dual-arm treatment-trajectory diagnostics or horizon-linked attenuation simulation. No 2024–2026 paper was found that (i) evaluates a field convention for publishing initiation trajectories beside the ITT estimate, (ii) defines a horizon rule for when the strategies remain distinct enough, or (iii) ships a validated simulation tool mapping observed convergence rates to expected attenuation at each horizon. Proposal and restatement are not resolution. Convergence remains a feature of the ITT strategy contrast under later initiation; PP or dynamic redesigns answer a different question. Status therefore remains open as stated. Queries run: observational ITT attenuation/dilution with later initiation and comparator crossover; target trial emulation treatment trajectories and cumulative initiation in both arms; TARGET/Cashin/Hansford reporting items on adherence and trajectories; Cain/Hernán prior art on dynamic strategies and ITT analogues; arXiv/medRxiv 2024–2026 TTE ITT crossover; CRAN/GitHub activity for TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, lmtp and related packages; FDA/EMA/NICE/ENCePP/STaRT-RWE/HARPER 2024–2026 guidance on adherence and ITT in observational emulations.

glm

open / supported. The statement is internally consistent and correctly identifies a structural feature of the observational ITT analogue (convergence of strategies over time) rather than a removable bias. The reason given for the problem being open—that convergence is intrinsic to the strategy contrast, rarely reported, and lacks a convention for horizon selection—actually supports its open status. The scope is appropriate: it correctly limits the claim to the ITT analogue and acknowledges that dynamic strategies (per-protocol) are a design response, not a fix for the ITT contrast itself. The severity is proportionate because an unreported convergence can lead to a misinterpretation of a null result.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2/4) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2/4)
