title: There is no theory for extrapolating successful replication of selected trials to new questions
text: BEN-01 Overstated Very high priority Established Tractability 3/5

title: There is no theory for extrapolating successful replication of selected trials to new questions
text:
Statement
A successful replication calibrates one emulation of one trial in one database. Transferring that confidence to a different question, or to the same question in a different database, is not an inference the benchmarking design licenses: it requires a target performance estimand stated in advance, an explicit selection or transport model, conditional exchangeability across the questions being compared, and overlap in whatever modifies emulation quality. Outside that support the transfer is model-dependent rather than identified, and frameworks that have been proposed for it remain unevaluated in that role. The benchmarking corpus is also a selected sample: trials get emulated when they are recent, large and have an accessible active comparator, which are the conditions under which emulation works best. Across 107 paired emulations and trials the effect correlation was 0.59 overall and 0.83 among the 63 pairs judged to emulate more closely, which measures performance on that favorable subpopulation and not on the questions a decision maker actually brings.

title: There is no theory for extrapolating successful replication of selected trials to new questions
text:
Why it is open
The benchmarking set is not a random sample of questions, and no design would make it one: a trial has to exist before it can be emulated, and the trials that exist are not the questions for which trials do not. Attributing a discrepancy requires knowing which of six candidate causes produced it, and the data that would separate them, particularly the trial’s own adherence and measurement, are usually unavailable to the emulator. Publishing after the trial result is known also creates design-calibration and selective-reporting risks that a concordance statistic cannot see, and only a prospective design removes them.

title: There is no theory for extrapolating successful replication of selected trials to new questions
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Wang SV, Schneeweiss S, RCT-DUPLICATE Initiative. Emulation of randomized clinical trials with nonrandomized database analyses: results of 32 clinical trials. JAMA 2023;329(16):1376-1385
The largest prespecified benchmarking program: 32 trials emulated in claims data with agreement reported against the trial results.


Concordance between target trial emulation and randomised controlled trials: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ 2025
Pools 107 emulation-trial pairs, reporting correlation 0.59 overall and 0.83 among closer emulations, and links poorer concordance to baseline imbalance, hospital-initiated treatment and inferior outcome emulation.

title: There is no theory for extrapolating successful replication of selected trials to new questions
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend prospective, blinded benchmarking, in which the emulation protocol and code are frozen and registered before the trial reports, from the isolated instances that now exist to a standing suite. Model concordance hierarchically by data source, clinical setting, outcome type and degree of protocol match, so what is estimated is a conditional expectation of agreement rather than a global rate, and state the target performance estimand before the comparison rather than after. Treat benchmarking as calibration evidence about a data source and a design class, never as certification of a method.

title: There is no theory for extrapolating successful replication of selected trials to new questions
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. A successful replication identifies calibration only for the evaluated trial, protocol, and database. Quantitative transfer to another question or database requires a prespecified target performance estimand, an explicit selection or transport model, conditional exchangeability, and overlap in relevant modifiers; outside that support, transfer is model-dependent rather than identified.
The source said. “Agreement between an emulation and a randomized trial raises confidence, and disagreement can arise from emulation failure, random error, different adherence, different measurement, different populations, or a limitation of the trial itself. RCT-DUPLICATE and the 2026 concordance meta-analysis both show better agreement under closer emulation and neither shows equivalence: across 107 paired emulations and trials the effect correlation was 0.59 overall and 0.83 among the 63 pairs judged to emulate more closely. What no one has is a theory that licenses the inference from those results to a new question: how much confidence a successful replication of trial A in database D transfers to question B in database D, or to question A in database E. Publishing after the trial result is known also creates design-calibration and selective-reporting risks that the concordance statistic cannot see.”
What was wrong with it. The claim that no theory exists was too strong in one direction and too weak in another. Frameworks for transferring benchmarking confidence have been proposed and are unevaluated for that role, so the honest statement is that transfer is model-dependent rather than unattempted. The entry also treated prospective blinded benchmarking as an untried proposal; it has been done at least once.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported-with-caveat): The entry proposes prospective, blinded benchmarking in which the protocol is frozen before the trial reports. That design now has at least one instance: a 2026 Circulation paper emulates a reference trial to predict the results of COBRRA before the trial’s result was available. So the proposal is not untried and the entry should say so. The theoretical claim survives intact: nothing licenses the inference from a successful replication in one database to a new question or a new database, and the concordance meta-analysis reports determinants of emulation success without supplying that extrapolation. One correction the entry must carry: the meta-analysis it cites has a published erratum, so any figure quoted from it needs checking against the corrected version. Supporting quotation retained here rather than as counter-evidence: [10.1136/bmj-2026-100303] Published Erratum to the concordance systematic review and meta-analysis. Any figure the entry quotes from that paper must be checked against the corrected version before publication.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The entry proposes prospective, blinded benchmarking in which the protocol is frozen before the trial reports. That design now has at least one instance: a 2026 Circulation paper emulates a reference trial to predict the results of COBRRA before the trial’s result was available. So the proposal is not untried and the entry should say so. The theoretical claim survives intact: nothing licenses the inference from a successful replication in one database to a new question or a new database, and the concordance meta-analysis reports determinants of emulation success without supplying that extrapolation. One correction the entry must carry: the meta-analysis it cites has a published erratum, so any figure quoted from it needs checking against the corrected version. Supporting quotation retained here rather than as counter-evidence: [10.1136/bmj-2026-100303] Published Erratum to the concordance systematic review and meta-analysis. Any figure the entry quotes from that paper must be checked against the corrected version before publication. Cites 10.1161/circoutcomes.125.012892: A prospective emulation issued as a prediction of a trial’s result, which is the blinded benchmarking design the entry proposes as future work.. Cites 10.1136/bmj-2025-086810: Supplies the concordance estimates and their determinants across paired emulations and trials..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The narrow identification concern is correct: performance on selected trial-database pairs does not nonparametrically identify performance for a new question or database without a defined target distribution, a sampling or selection model, conditional exchangeability of benchmark performance, and positivity over the relevant design and setting modifiers. The assertion that there is “no theory” or “no design” is too absolute. Transport and hierarchical prediction are possible under explicit assumptions, although a hierarchical model cannot identify extrapolation outside observed support merely by conditioning on study features. Correlation is also not an agreement measure: it can be high despite systematic bias and low because of restricted effect variation or sampling error. Freezing the protocol prospectively blocks outcome-informed design adaptation only if all analytic choices are locked; it does not by itself prevent selective reporting after unblinding. The problem remains open in its narrower form because the supplied agenda does not provide an identified and validated transfer procedure. Its very-high severity is warranted only when benchmarking is used to certify decisions beyond the benchmarked design class.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

partially-solved / overstated. Inverted prior favors solutions that license transfer of successful A-in-D replications to B-in-D or A-in-E. BenchExCal (Wang et al. 2025) is exactly that transfer procedure for indication expansion: benchmark an existing-indication trial in the database, then calibrate a subsequent database study for the expanded question using the observed RCT–database differences. Kirchgesner et al. (2024) state a related trial-calibration approach for questions RCTs never answered. Heyard et al. (2024) and the BMJ 2026 concordance meta-analysis already move from a global agreement rate toward design-conditional agreement (protocol match, baseline balance, outcome quality, claims vs other sources). Prospective prediction projects (GRADE, semaglutide phase IV, FDA prediction workstream) partially remove design-calibration by freezing protocols before trial readout. None of this is a completed, general statistical theory that quantifies how much confidence transfers to arbitrary new questions or databases, and BenchExCal’s empirical evaluation is still planned (simulation plus five examples), not finished. The six-cause attribution problem for single discrepancies remains open. Saying there is “no theory” is therefore too strong; the gap is the lack of a validated general theory and completed prospective hierarchical calibration, not a blank slate. Cites 10.1002/cpt.3621: Proposes an operational theory for transferring a successful existing-indication emulation (question A in database D) into a calibrated second-stage emulation for an expanded indication (question B in D), with simulation and five planned empirical evaluations. Directly addresses the report’s missing transfer step, though as proposal plus planned evaluation rather than finished validation.. Cites 10.1002/pds.70008: Articulates trial calibration as the route from benchmarked emulation of an answered question to RWE on a related unanswered question, the same transfer structure the problem says is missing.. Cites 10.1136/bmjmed-2023-000709: Models concordance variation as a function of design and population emulation differences rather than a single global rate, which is the hierarchical/conditional direction the report proposes.. Cites 10.1136/bmj-2025-086810: Estimates design-conditional concordance (closer emulation; baseline imbalance; hospital-initiated treatment; outcome emulation quality; claims data) across 107 pairs, so agreement is already treated as a conditional quantity, not only a global rate. Does not solve transfer to unselected questions..

glm

open / supported. The claim is internally consistent and proportionate. It correctly identifies a structural gap: existing benchmarking provides empirical concordance on a favorable subpopulation but lacks a formal theory for extrapolating this to new questions or databases. The reasons given (non-random sampling of trials, multiple confounding causes for discrepancies) directly support why the problem remains open. The claim is appropriately scoped as a limitation of current methodological frameworks rather than an impossibility.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2/4) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2/4)

title: Open Problems in Target Trial Emulation
text:
Target trial emulation gave observational comparative effectiveness research a discipline it lacked: state the protocol of the randomized trial you would have run, then say exactly how each component is emulated in the data you have. That discipline removed a class of self-inflicted errors. It did not remove the rest.
This site catalogs the open problems, one entry at a time. Each says what the problem is, why it stays open, what has already been tried, and the most probable route to a solution.

title: Open Problems in Target Trial Emulation
text:
Start here


Browse the catalog
Every problem in one filterable table. Sort by priority, filter by category or verdict, or search across all fields.


The prioritized agenda
What should change in practice now, what should be built next, and what is high-risk and high-reward.


The method landscape
What each approach identifies, where it breaks, and a decision path from an emulation problem to a defensible method.


How this was verified
The provenance of this material, the audit protocol, and an honest account of what the verdicts do and do not establish.

title: Open Problems in Target Trial Emulation
text:
The organizing distinction
The decisive division is between problems a complete protocol specification solves and problems that survive a perfect protocol.
Writing the protocol down is what defeats misalignment of eligibility, assignment and the start of follow-up, and with it immortal time bias. Those problems are, in principle, bookkeeping: they are caused by the analyst and fixed by the analyst. The catalog records them because applied practice still gets them wrong, not because the theory is missing.
Everything else survives. A protocol states which confounders you intend to adjust for; it cannot make them measured. It states a sustained strategy; it cannot make that strategy achievable in people whose covariate history never receives it. It names an outcome; it cannot make the phenotype algorithm that ascertains the outcome correct. Most of the hardest entries here sit on that side of the line.
Three consequences run through the whole collection.
Emulation prevents self-inflicted bias; it does not create randomization. An immaculately aligned time zero and an active-comparator new-user design remove specific, nameable errors. They leave exchangeability exactly where it was: an assumption, untestable from the data being analyzed. Covariate balance after weighting is evidence about the variables you measured and silent about the ones you did not.
Choices made before any model is fitted cannot be priced by the model. The grace period, the time grid, the lookback window, the code list defining the outcome: each is fixed before estimation, and each changes the estimand rather than merely the precision. No amount of flexibility in the nuisance models recovers a choice made upstream of them.
Agreement with a randomized trial is calibration evidence, not certification. When an emulation and its index trial disagree, the candidates are residual confounding, a different population, differently measured exposure or outcome, a different estimand, and chance. Nothing in the current toolkit separates them for the single study in front of a decision maker.

title: Open Problems in Target Trial Emulation
text:
Reading a verdict
Every entry carries a verdict recording what happened when its claims were checked against the literature and against independent external auditors. A verdict of Overstated does not mean the problem is not real; it usually means the underlying issue is real and a claim about its severity was pitched too strongly. Entries marked Resolved since report are kept rather than deleted, because knowing that something was recently closed is as useful as knowing it is open.
The source material for this catalog was produced by a large language model and then audited. How this was verified explains what that means in practice, including where the audit’s own limits are.

title: How this was verified
text:
This catalog is derived from a deep-research document produced by a large language model (ChatGPT deep research) in July 2026, covering open methodological, theoretical, practical, data-related and interpretive problems in target trial emulation.
That origin is the reason this page exists. A machine-generated research agenda is a plausible-sounding artifact whether or not it is correct, and publishing one as settled fact would be a disservice. Nothing from the source document appears on this site without a verification verdict attached, and the evidence behind each verdict is shown on the entry itself.
The source document is kept as working material and is not published here.


The source was supplied in three formats. The markdown export had lost every citation. ChatGPT’s markdown export replaces each link with private-use-area characters and an opaque handle, so the exported file contained 125 citation tokens, zero DOIs, zero URLs, and zero PubMed identifiers. The .docx of the same document retained the real hyperlinks.
Extraction therefore runs from the .docx, not the export. That distinction is not cosmetic: had the markdown been used, every entry in this catalog would have been unsourced, and the audit would have had nothing to check a citation against.

title: How this was verified
text:
The audit
Every problem was assessed as a whole statement rather than decomposed into atomic claims, because the statements are written to be falsifiable in one piece: each names a specific thing that does not exist. Four auditors assessed each entry independently, and each returned two votes, one on whether the problem is still open and one on whether the claim as written is faithful and proportionate, together with the weakest version of the claim they would still defend. Those weakest restatements are what the published statement was rewritten to.

Literature verification
For each problem, every cited work was checked to confirm it supports the claim attributed to it, and the screened corpus on this site was searched for later work that would resolve or narrow the problem. The search ran against the 1,376 records held locally rather than against recall, so every locator in a verification opinion is a record that exists in the collection and can be opened. Where the search found nothing, the opinion says so and its confidence is capped, because absence from one corpus of PubMed and PMC records is weak evidence of absence in the field.


Adversarial refutation
The adversarial lens is one of the independent auditors rather than a separate pass. It is given an inverted prior: assume the problem has already been solved, and go find who solved it. Asking a model to confirm a claim and asking it to break the claim produce different results, and only the second is informative.
The sibling project this pipeline was ported from declares a separate refuting auditor in its adjudication rule that casts no opinions, which leaves one guard in that rule permanently inert. Rather than reproduce a lens that is named and does not run, the roster here names only auditors that vote, and the rule counts only those.


Independent external auditors
Frontier models outside this system were given the same claims, blind to each other and to the literature pass, each with a different lens:

a technical and source-code lens, which checks identification arguments, weight algebra, cloning and censoring bookkeeping, and immortal-time accounting, and which verifies any claim about a software package against that package’s pinned source rather than against the report;
a recency and prior-art lens, which adopts an inverted prior. It assumes each problem has already been solved and goes looking for who solved it, because an agenda that lists a solved problem as open is the most damaging error this site can make: the people most likely to read it are the people who solved it;
a third independent lens on the same claims, so that a majority is a majority of more than two.

Each entry’s page lists the auditors that voted on it. Coverage is not uniform. External models run out of quota mid-run, and one of them intermittently returns a well-formed but empty verdict for a batch, answering in about a hundred tokens where a real assessment takes several thousand. Those batches are detected and re-run rather than counted as complete, and the ones that stay empty after a re-run leave the entry adjudicated by fewer auditors. Where that happened the page says so, rather than presenting a thinner audit as an equal one, and every majority rule is taken over the auditors that actually voted on that entry.


Adjudication
Opinions become a published verdict by a fixed rule, not by judgment. The rule records its own decision path on every entry, so the route from votes to verdict is visible.
Two principles govern it:
A “solved” vote without a locator is not evidence. It is downgraded rather than counted. An auditor asserting that something has been solved must name the work that solved it.
Evidence beats votes. A lone dissenter holding an unrebutted verbatim quote is not silently outvoted by auditors holding opinions.
Majority rules carry a denominator. A verdict such as Overstated requires at least two independent auditors and at least half of the auditors that actually returned an opinion on that entry. Using the roster size as the denominator would let an entry reached by two auditors be decided on the same evidence as one reached by four.

title: How this was verified
section: Which fields are audited, and which are editorial
text:
Which fields are audited, and which are editorial
This distinction matters and is easy to lose.
Audited. The statement, why it is open, the prior work, and the extracted claims. These went through literature verification, adversarial refutation and the independent auditors, and they carry the verdict.
Editorial. Maturity, tractability, severity, the proposed research direction, and the protocol-component and data-setting tags. These are one reader’s judgment applied to make the catalog browsable. They were not audited and should not be cited as findings. The proposed direction in particular reads with the same visual authority as the audited statement above it, and it is a research suggestion rather than a verified claim.
Deliberately rebuilt. Priority is not carried over from the source. It reflects three observable things: whether the problem blocks a decision-grade estimand, whether any method addresses it at all, and whether any software implements it.

title: How this was verified
section: What the verdicts do not mean
text:
What the verdicts do not mean
A verdict is a judgment about a claim, not about a problem’s importance.
Overstated almost never means the problem is fictional. It usually means the underlying difficulty is real and the source pitched its severity, or the claim that no method exists, more strongly than the evidence supports. The entry records the strongest version of the claim that survived.
Confirmed open means the checks agreed and no counterevidence surfaced. It does not mean nobody is working on it, and it is a statement about the literature that was reachable, not about the literature that exists.
Unverifiable means the auditors disagreed with evidence on both sides, or that no accessible source could settle it. The disagreement is shown on the entry rather than resolved silently.

title: How this was verified
text:
Limits of this exercise
This is not a systematic review. There was no protocol registration, no duplicate independent screening with a reported agreement statistic, and no formal risk-of-bias assessment.
The literature harvest covers PubMed and PubMed Central only. Conference abstracts and journals indexed in Embase but not PubMed are missing. Embase has no API available without a subscription.
The auditors are language models. They are better at finding a paper that closes a gap than at proving no such paper exists, so Confirmed open carries less weight than Resolved since report. A confirmed absence of evidence is the weakest thing on this site.

title: How this was verified
text:
Reproducing this
Everything is in the repository. build/render_site.mjs turns the registry into these pages, build/make_audit_batches.mjs produces the auditor prompts, and build/adjudicate.mjs applies the rule. documentation/audit/calibration.json holds known-answer cases verified by hand; any audit configuration that fails to reproduce them is miscalibrated, and they are asserted before the site is built.

title: Studies
text:
The catalog records what is open. This is the attempt to close some of it: one study a week, each aimed at a single entry, taken in priority order.
Scope is target trial emulation only: the specification of an emulated protocol, the g-methods used to estimate the effects of sustained treatment strategies, and the benchmarking of emulations against the trials they emulate. A problem that would be the same problem in any observational analysis is out of scope, because it is not what this catalog is about.

title: Studies
text:
How a problem gets chosen
Not every open problem can be settled by a study, and the difference is not cosmetic. A simulation can measure bias, coverage and error rates, and it can show how badly a known nonidentification bites at realistic sample sizes. It cannot establish that a package is missing, that clinicians misread a plot, that a field under-reports something, or that a quantity is unidentifiable in principle. Those need software, a case study, a meta-research corpus, or a proof.
Every one of the 0 catalog entries was judged on both questions separately, by an external model, before the program started: is this a target trial emulation problem, and what kind of study would settle it. The queue below is the intersection.

title: Studies
section: What each study has to do
text:
What each study has to do
Simulation studies follow ADEMP: aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods, performance measures (Morris, White and Crowther 2019). Two rules follow from it and are enforced rather than encouraged.

Every performance measure carries a Monte Carlo standard error.

A bias of 0.02 is uninterpretable without knowing whether the Monte Carlo error is 0.001 or 0.03. The replicate count is derived in the protocol from a target Monte Carlo standard error, not chosen because it is a round number.

Failed replicates are results.

A method that converges on 60% of replicates and is unbiased on those is not an unbiased method. Convergence is reported for every method in every scenario.

The protocol is committed before the run.

It fixes the design and states in advance what result would count as showing the problem is real and what would count as showing it is not. The commit that adds it is the timestamp.


Code, protocols and results are at github.com/choxos/TTE-open-problems/tree/main/studies.

title: Replication is reported as a binary label rather than as a calibrated comparison of estimands
text: BEN-02 Overstated High priority Established Tractability 5/5

title: Replication is reported as a binary label rather than as a calibrated comparison of estimands
text:
Statement
Agreement between an emulation and a trial is informative only when the estimands, populations and measurements are close enough to be comparable, and better design alignment is empirically associated with stronger concordance. The benchmarking programs report this in graded form. What is cited downstream is a binary label, usually derived from interval overlap or direction agreement, and that label discards magnitude and uncertainty and cannot diagnose why two estimates differ: two studies estimating the same quantity imprecisely agree by that criterion, and two estimating different quantities precisely disagree. No reported measure, graded or binary, separates estimand mismatch from random error, because doing so requires aligning the estimands first and then reporting a paired contrast with joint uncertainty, which no benchmarking report currently does as a matter of course.

title: Replication is reported as a binary label rather than as a calibrated comparison of estimands
text:
Why it is open
Separating estimand mismatch from random error requires a distributional claim about the trial’s own error that trials do not publish, so the criterion that would do it cannot be computed from what is available. Aligning estimands before comparison is possible and expensive, and it reduces the number of comparable pairs, which is the resource benchmarking is short of. The binary label is also convenient for the audiences who cite benchmarking results, so the pressure to replace it runs the wrong way.

title: Replication is reported as a binary label rather than as a calibrated comparison of estimands
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Wang SV, Schneeweiss S, RCT-DUPLICATE Initiative. Emulation of randomized clinical trials with nonrandomized database analyses: results of 32 clinical trials. JAMA 2023;329(16):1376-1385
Reports agreement across 32 prespecified emulations using several agreement metrics, which is the most careful existing treatment of the labeling question.


Concordance between target trial emulation and randomised controlled trials: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ 2025
Reports effect correlation and standardized-difference agreement across 107 pairs and relates concordance to specific design features rather than to a pass or fail label.

title: Replication is reported as a binary label rather than as a calibrated comparison of estimands
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Align estimands before comparing, then report the paired contrast with joint uncertainty, heterogeneity and any prespecified tolerance that a categorical judgment would rest on, so a pass or fail is derived rather than assumed. Report ratio of effects, absolute effect difference, standardized agreement and prediction-interval coverage together, so estimand mismatch and random error remain separately visible. Prefer prospective forecasts of a trial’s result to retrospective comparison, and replicate across databases as well as across questions, since a data source’s calibration is what a decision maker needs.

title: Replication is reported as a binary label rather than as a calibrated comparison of estimands
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Binary replication labels based on interval overlap or effect direction discard magnitude and uncertainty and cannot diagnose why estimates differ. Decision-grade benchmarking should first align estimands, then report paired contrasts with joint uncertainty, heterogeneity, and prespecified tolerances whenever a categorical judgment is required.
The source said. “Agreement between an emulation and a trial is informative only when the estimands, populations and measurements are close enough to be comparable, and better design alignment is empirically associated with stronger concordance. Benchmarking nonetheless reports success or failure as a binary label, usually derived from whether the confidence intervals overlap or whether the direction agrees. That label mixes estimand mismatch with random error: two studies estimating the same quantity with wide intervals will agree by that criterion, and two estimating different quantities precisely will disagree. The reported statistic therefore does not measure what its users take it to measure.”
What was wrong with it. The entry attributed the binary label to the benchmarking programs. They do not use one: RCT-DUPLICATE reports several agreement metrics and the 2026 concordance meta-analysis reports correlation and standardized agreement related to design features. The reduction to pass or fail happens downstream, in how those results are cited, which is a different and narrower claim.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): The entry criticizes binary replication labels. The concordance meta-analysis it draws on does not use one: it reports correlation and standardized-difference agreement and relates them to design features, which is the graded reporting the entry asks for. RCT-DUPLICATE similarly reports several agreement metrics. So the criticism lands on the citing practice rather than on the benchmarking literature, and the entry should say that. The part that survives is that a graded criterion still does not separate estimand mismatch from random error, since prediction-interval coverage requires a distributional claim about the trial’s own error that trials do not publish.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. The entry criticizes binary replication labels. The concordance meta-analysis it draws on does not use one: it reports correlation and standardized-difference agreement and relates them to design features, which is the graded reporting the entry asks for. RCT-DUPLICATE similarly reports several agreement metrics. So the criticism lands on the citing practice rather than on the benchmarking literature, and the entry should say that. The part that survives is that a graded criterion still does not separate estimand mismatch from random error, since prediction-interval coverage requires a distributional claim about the trial’s own error that trials do not publish. Cites 10.1001/jama.2023.4221: Reports multiple agreement metrics rather than a single binary label.. Cites 10.1136/bmj-2025-086810: Reports correlation and standardized agreement and relates both to design features, which is graded rather than binary..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. The criticism of confidence-interval overlap and sign agreement is technically sound, but the problem is framed too broadly. The agenda’s own descriptions say that the cited benchmarks already report several graded metrics, including effect correlation and standardized differences, so benchmarking is not uniformly binary. Continuous effect differences, ratios, and standardized contrasts still cannot separate estimand mismatch from random error. That separation first requires commensurate estimands and then a joint sampling model incorporating uncertainty from both estimates, their covariance when applicable, and between-pair heterogeneity. Prediction-interval coverage does not require a trial to publish a full error distribution when an estimate and standard error or confidence interval are available, and coverage is itself calibrated across a suite rather than diagnosed from one pair. Ratios are additionally unstable when the reference effect is near zero. This is therefore partly an implementation and reporting problem with existing tools, not wholly an unresolved statistical-method problem; high severity is disproportionate unless the binary label is the sole basis for a decision. Cites 10.1001/jama.2023.4221: As characterized in the batch, this program reports several agreement metrics rather than only a binary replication label, partially resolving the reporting problem while not separating all sources of discrepancy.. Cites 10.1136/bmj-2025-086810: As characterized in the batch, this analysis reports effect correlation and standardized-difference agreement across pairs and evaluates design-related variation, partially addressing graded comparison..

Grok 4.5, recency lens

partially-solved / overstated. The claim that benchmarking “nonetheless reports success or failure as a binary label” is not faithful to the field’s primary programs or to the report’s own cited works. RCT-DUPLICATE and Franklin-line methods report regulatory/significance agreement, estimate agreement, and standardized-difference agreement together; the BMJ 2026 meta-analysis leads with Pearson correlation, ICC, ratio of ratios, standardized-difference agreement, and Bland–Altman, and only secondarily with binary metrics. Köppe, Micheloud, Erdmann, Heyard, and Held (2025) go further: they replace the two-trials (regulatory agreement) rule with the graded sceptical p-value, which uses both p-values, effect sizes, and relative precision, and invert it to combined confidence intervals; they apply it to 29 RCT-DUPLICATE pairs. ISPOR Europe 2024 also floated enhanced multi-metric RCT–RWE agreement assessments for HTA. What remains open is universal adoption, explicit estimand alignment (how much estimand difference is tolerable), and routine prediction-interval coverage that treats trial sampling error as a distribution. Binary labels are still convenient for secondary citation and still appear beside continuous metrics, but they are not the sole or best existing practice. The report’s proposed direction (ratio of effects, absolute difference, standardized agreement, prediction-interval coverage, prospective forecasts) is largely what the better literature already does or is building. Cites 10.1001/jama.2023.4221: Already reports multiple agreement metrics (not a single pass/fail label) across 32 prespecified emulations; this is the report’s own cited “most careful existing treatment of the labeling question.”. Cites 10.1136/bmj-2025-086810: Primary reporting is continuous and multi-metric (correlation 0.59/0.83, ratio of ratios, standardized-difference rates, design-feature regressions), not a binary success label. Directly undercuts the claim that benchmarking only reports binary agreement.. Cites arxiv:2412.09334: Supplies a graded, calibrated alternative to binary two-trials/regulatory agreement (the sceptical p-value), depending on both p-values, effect sizes, and relative precision; extends to non-inferiority and inverted CIs; applied to RCT-DUPLICATE. Partially delivers the report’s call for calibrated comparison rather than a binary label.. Cites 10.1186/s12874-025-02589-z: Peer-reviewed publication of the sceptical p-value application to RWE emulations (same work as arXiv 2412.09334), confirming the graded metric is in the methods literature, not only a preprint..

glm

open / supported. The claim is internally consistent and proportionate. It accurately characterizes a limitation in current practice: benchmarking often relies on binary labels (e.g., CI overlap) that conflate estimand mismatch with random error. The stated reasons for it being open (the difficulty of defining tolerable estimand differences and the convenience of binary labels) logically support the persistence of this practice. The claim is appropriately scoped as a critique of current reporting standards rather than an impossibility claim.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2/4) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2/4)

title: Data-fitness assessment is narrative and has no thresholds that would stop a study
text: DTA-01 Overstated Very high priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: Data-fitness assessment is narrative and has no thresholds that would stop a study
text:
Statement
Electronic health records arise from encounters, billing and documentation rather than from scheduled research assessments, so eligibility and follow-up in an emulation partly reflect care-seeking and access rather than the biology the protocol intends. Whether a given database can support a given target trial is a question about the data source and the protocol jointly, and quantitative assessments of that pair now exist. What does not exist is a prespecified stop rule: a threshold agreed before the analysis, on observability, temporal precision, capture continuity, comparator support, outcome validity and linkage completeness, that would halt a study when an essential component fails. Outside tightly gated regulatory and network feasibility processes, most published emulations still assert suitability in a paragraph, and a pipeline with no route to the answer no will always produce an estimate.

title: Data-fitness assessment is narrative and has no thresholds that would stop a study
text:
Why it is open
Fitness is a property of the pair formed by the data and the protocol, so a fixed score is the wrong object and any threshold has to be estimand- and decision-specific, which makes standardization hard rather than merely unattempted. Validating a threshold against trial concordance is the obvious route and does not work on its own, because the benchmarking corpus is a selected sample of favorable questions. And any threshold that would stop a study costs someone a publication, while no external body currently imposes one.

title: Data-fitness assessment is narrative and has no thresholds that would stop a study
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Wang, et al. An operational target trial emulation framework for causal inference using electronic health records. npj Digit Med 2026
Sets out the operational constraints electronic health records place on each protocol component, which is the raw material a fitness score would formalize.


NICE real-world evidence framework
States that some target trials cannot be adequately emulated with available data and that bespoke data collection may be preferable, which is the design-failure outcome this problem wants to make operational.

title: Data-fitness assessment is narrative and has no thresholds that would stop a study
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build trial-component fitness scores computed against the specific protocol rather than against the database in the abstract, and state the decision they serve, so the threshold is defensible for that decision rather than universal. Predefine stop rules and publish the fitness report whether or not the study proceeds, which is what turns a negative assessment into a citable result. Validate the scores against concordance while stating what that validation cannot establish, since a corpus of emulable questions cannot calibrate a rule meant to identify inemulable ones.

title: Data-fitness assessment is narrative and has no thresholds that would stop a study
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Many target-trial emulations lack prespecified, protocol-specific quantitative adequacy criteria and no-go rules. Transparent component-level assessments could improve decisions about whether to proceed, but thresholds must be estimand- and decision-specific, and randomized-trial concordance alone cannot validate them.
The source said. “Electronic health records arise from encounters, billing and documentation rather than from scheduled research assessments, so eligibility and follow-up in an emulation partly reflect care-seeking and access rather than the biology the protocol intends. Whether a given database can support a given target trial is therefore a question about the data source and the trial jointly. In practice this is answered narratively, in a paragraph asserting that the data are suitable, with no quantitative thresholds and no procedure that could return the answer no. A pipeline that cannot conclude that the trial is not emulable will always produce an estimate, and the estimate will not carry the fact that the question could not be asked.”
What was wrong with it. Quantitative data-quality assessment for emulation exists and is being formalized, including an assessment of record and linked-claims data built for emulation studies specifically, so the claim that the question is answered only narratively was too strong. What is absent is narrower: prespecified stop rules, and a route by which a negative assessment becomes a published result rather than a private decision.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported-with-caveat): The entry says data-fitness assessment is narrative with no quantitative thresholds. A 2026 JAMIA Open paper assesses the quality of electronic health record data and linked claims data specifically for target trial emulation studies, which is a quantitative fitness assessment for this purpose and not a narrative one. Regulatory syntheses for GLP-1 therapies and oncology reviews also set out data-adequacy considerations. What none supplies is the predefined stop rule the entry asks for, or the publication of a negative fitness assessment as a citable result, so the operational half of the claim stands and the descriptive half is too strong.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The entry says data-fitness assessment is narrative with no quantitative thresholds. A 2026 JAMIA Open paper assesses the quality of electronic health record data and linked claims data specifically for target trial emulation studies, which is a quantitative fitness assessment for this purpose and not a narrative one. Regulatory syntheses for GLP-1 therapies and oncology reviews also set out data-adequacy considerations. What none supplies is the predefined stop rule the entry asks for, or the publication of a negative fitness assessment as a citable result, so the operational half of the claim stands and the descriptive half is too strong. Cites 10.1093/jamiaopen/ooag102: Assesses data quality for the emulation purpose specifically, which is the fitness assessment the entry says does not exist quantitatively.. Cites 10.7326/annals-26-00202: Sets out data-adequacy considerations for a high-stakes therapeutic area where emulation is being used for decisions..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The residual problem is real: data fitness is specific to the protocol, estimand, and decision context, and prespecified component-level no-go criteria would improve study governance. The statement nevertheless overstates the absence of quantitative assessment. Availability, temporal resolution, treatment support, follow-up continuity, outcome capture, and validation performance can all be measured, although they do not collapse into a universally valid score. External validation data are not required for every fitness component. A pipeline without explicit stop rules also does not necessarily always return an estimate, while an estimator’s standard error generally will not represent bias from nonidentification or poor measurement. Benchmark concordance cannot by itself validate a fitness score because disagreement can arise from estimand differences, transportability, adherence, measurement, or bias in either study. This is decision-critical when an essential protocol component is unobservable or unsupported; otherwise, standardized scoring and publication of assessments are primarily governance and reproducibility improvements.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

partially-solved / overstated. Inverted-prior search finds substantial prior art that already structures protocol-paired data fitness and can return no, so the claim that fitness is only a narrative paragraph with no thresholds and no procedure that can stop a study is overstated. SPIFD (2021) and SPIFD2 (2023) are step-by-step feasibility frameworks that pair research question, target-trial articulation, and data-source selection, with component-level documentation and heatmaps intended to support go or no-go decisions before estimation. The CARE oncology work (Levy et al., 2026) runs a systematic multi-stage fitness screen over six commercial EHR sources and 23 candidate RCTs: of 54 RCT-RWD combinations, nine reached detailed feasibility and only three were selected for emulation protocol development, with explicit fitness constraints (complex eligibility, biomarkers, performance status, outcome ascertainment). OHDSI DataQualityDashboard implements quantitative pass/fail thresholds on CDM conformance, and DARWIN EU study phases include a feasibility assessment that issues a recommendation on whether to conduct the study. Lee et al. (2026) quantifies TTE-relevant completeness, accuracy, plausibility, and concordance for an EHR cohort against Medicare claims, and Wang et al. (2026) formalizes when EHR realization of trial components can or cannot yield interpretable estimates. What remains open is exactly the hard part of the proposed agenda: field-standard, protocol-component fitness scores with pre-specified stop rules that academic pipelines cannot bypass; routine publication of negative fitness assessments as citable results; and empirical validation that low fitness predicts poor concordance with the corresponding trial. Regulatory and industry pathways already gate more often than the report implies; general-purpose TTE software (TrialEmulation and related packages) still does not enforce a fitness gate that returns no. Cites 10.1002/cpt.70310: Demonstrates a systematic multi-stage, protocol-paired fitness assessment that rates RCT design elements for availability, missingness, and validity and that stops most candidate emulations: 54 RCT-RWD combinations narrowed to nine detailed assessments and three selected for protocol development.. Cites 10.1002/cpt.2883: Provides a structured, documentable process that pairs target-trial articulation with data-source fitness assessment and is intended to identify when design and data are not decision-grade before estimation proceeds.. Cites 10.1093/jamia/ocab132: Implements quantitative data-quality checks with configurable decision thresholds (OHDSI DataQualityDashboard) that can return pass or fail; covers CDM structural and value-level quality rather than full protocol-component TTE fitness, but disproves the claim that no thresholded procedure exists.. Cites 10.64898/2025.12.22.25342844: Quantifies TTE-relevant data quality (completeness, accuracy, plausibility, concordance) for eligibility, exposure, covariates, outcomes, and follow-up in EHR-only versus claims-linked data; shows a quantitative fitness evaluation against a reference source, while still requiring that external validation source..

glm

open / supported. The claim is internally consistent and proportionate. It correctly frames data fitness as a joint property of the data source and the protocol, rather than the data alone. The assertion that current practice is narrative and lacks stop rules is a claim about current practice rather than a structural impossibility, and the reasons given for it being open (fitness is a pair property, thresholds cost publications, validation sources are rare) logically support the claim’s openness.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2/4) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2/4)

title: Common data models harmonize structure without guaranteeing that the same variable means the same thing
text: DTA-03 Confirmed open High priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: Common data models harmonize structure without guaranteeing that the same variable means the same thing
text:
Statement
Claims, records, registries, mortality files and laboratory data each carry part of what a protocol needs, and linking them changes both who is eligible and which outcomes are captured. Linkage is imperfect and coding systems change over time, so the same analytic variable can shift meaning across sites and across years within one site. Multi-source linked databases are associated with better emulation of trials, which makes linkage decisions consequential rather than administrative. Common data models solve the structural half and do not guarantee semantic equivalence, and the historical code mappings and extract versions that would let a reader check are rarely preserved in publications. Semantic drift is invisible in the analytic dataset, because the column is populated and the values are in range.

title: Common data models harmonize structure without guaranteeing that the same variable means the same thing
text:
Why it is open
Detecting drift requires the mapping history and a comparison across extracts, and both are normally discarded once the analytic file is built, so the evidence that would settle it is destroyed rather than merely unexamined. Linkage error is also non-random, correlating with the same social and health-system factors that predict treatment and outcome, which makes it a confounded measurement error rather than noise. And propagating linkage uncertainty correctly needs an explicit model of the linkage mechanism, which is exactly what a probabilistic linkage supplies only partially.

title: Common data models harmonize structure without guaranteeing that the same variable means the same thing
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Concordance between target trial emulation and randomised controlled trials: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ 2025
Finds that closer design emulation and better outcome emulation predict agreement with trials, and that claims-based emulations tended to underestimate trial effects, which is where data provenance becomes measurable.


Wang, et al. An operational target trial emulation framework for causal inference using electronic health records. npj Digit Med 2026
Sets out the operational mapping from source fields to protocol components, the level at which provenance would have to be recorded.

title: Common data models harmonize structure without guaranteeing that the same variable means the same thing
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Maintain provenance graphs from source field to analytic variable and publish them, so a reader can see which code set produced an outcome and when it changed. Run phenotype invariance and temporal-drift checks as standard diagnostics, and report leave-one-source-out analyses so each linked source’s contribution is visible. Propagate linkage uncertainty under stated assumptions about the linkage mechanism, and report a linkage sensitivity analysis rather than treating a probabilistic weight as though it converted bias into variance.

title: Common data models harmonize structure without guaranteeing that the same variable means the same thing
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Claims, records, registries, mortality files and laboratory data each carry part of what a protocol needs, and linking them changes both who is eligible and which outcomes are captured. Linkage is imperfect and coding systems change over time, so the same analytic variable can shift meaning across sites and across years within a site. Multi-source linked databases are associated with better emulation of trials, which makes the linkage decisions consequential rather than administrative. Common data models solve the structural half of this and do not guarantee semantic or causal equivalence, and the historical code mappings and extract versions that would let a reader check are rarely preserved in publications.”
What was wrong with it. The statement stands; the proposed direction did not. Carrying probabilistic linkage weights into the estimator does not turn linkage bias into variance and does not by itself guarantee unbiased estimation. Propagating linkage uncertainty requires stating the assumptions under which the propagation is valid.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. A search for linkage or common-data-model work addressing semantic drift, provenance graphs or phenotype invariance returned nothing in the screened corpus. The concordance meta-analysis provides indirect support by finding that claims-based emulations tended to underestimate trial effects and that outcome-emulation quality predicted agreement, which is the data-provenance channel operating without being measured directly. The absence is the evidence here, so the confidence is capped: informatics venues indexed outside these eight phrases would not have been retrieved.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. It is technically correct that a common data model standardizes representation without guaranteeing semantic, measurement, or causal equivalence. Versioned provenance and temporal validation are therefore important. Several stronger assertions are not generally correct. Semantic drift is not necessarily invisible in an analytic dataset; prevalence discontinuities, distribution shifts, coding transitions, and changes in associations can flag it, although provenance is usually needed to explain it. Linkage error is not inherently nonrandom and should not generically be called confounded measurement error: depending on the linkage mechanism, it can induce selection bias, exposure or outcome misclassification, or little bias. Most importantly, carrying probabilistic linkage weights into a causal estimator does not automatically convert hidden bias into interval width. That requires a calibrated linkage model, compatible integration with treatment and censoring estimation, and valid uncertainty propagation; differential or misspecified linkage can leave substantial bias. Provenance graphs, drift checks, and leave-one-source-out analyses are useful diagnostics but cannot prove semantic invariance or identify linkage bias by themselves. The issue is critical when key eligibility, treatment, confounder, or outcome variables are affected, but otherwise may be a robustness and provenance roadmap item.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. The core claim is still true and was not overturned by 2024-2026 literature or software: common data models (OMOP and peers) standardize structure and vocabulary mapping, but do not guarantee semantic or causal equivalence of analytic variables across sites or years, and the mapping history and extract versions needed to check drift are still rarely published with target trial emulations. TARGET (2025) improves reporting of how the trial protocol is mapped to observational data, and OHDSI tools (DataQualityDashboard, CohortDiagnostics, standardized vocabularies) improve structural quality and phenotype characterization, but neither certifies that the same column means the same clinical construct. Work that partially implements pieces of the proposed direction exists and should not be ignored: Guha and Reiter (2024) fuse Bayesian probabilistic record linkage with causal estimators so linkage uncertainty propagates into treatment-effect inference rather than being collapsed to a hard match (bipartite two-file setting, evaluated in simulation and survey data, not multi-source claims-EHR-registry TTE as standard practice); Johns, Baum, and Prasser (2025) track provenance through clinical-warehouse ETL for quality management; semi-automated linkage provenance prototypes appear in the data-linkage literature. Those are proposals or infrastructure for components of the agenda, not a solved provenance-plus-invariance-plus-leave-one-source-out standard for multi-source TTE. The BMJ 2025 concordance review supports that design and outcome emulation quality matter for trial agreement, which makes provenance consequential, but does not itself close the semantic-equivalence gap. Searches for phenotype temporal-drift diagnostics, published source-to-analytic provenance graphs in TTE, and routine leave-one-source-out multi-source analyses as standard practice returned methods papers and tools, not field resolution. Vote open; partial methods noted in rationale without over-crediting them as solutions.

glm

open / supported. The statement is internally consistent and correctly distinguishes structural harmonization from semantic equivalence. The claim that common data models solve the structural half without guaranteeing semantic equivalence is proportionate. The reasons provided for it being open (semantic drift is invisible in the analytic dataset, mapping histories are discarded, and linkage error is non-random) logically entail that the problem is currently open.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-overstatement(n=1/4):codex

title: Eligibility criteria built from healthcare-use variables can induce selection through colliders
text: ELG-02 Confirmed open Medium-high priority Speculative Tractability 3/5

title: Eligibility criteria built from healthcare-use variables can induce selection through colliders
text:
Statement
An eligibility criterion is a conditioning statement, and conditioning on a variable that is a collider, or a relevant descendant of one, in the graph relating determinants of treatment and outcome opens a noncausal path rather than closing one. Emulation protocols routinely build eligibility from healthcare-use variables: a required prior visit, a recorded baseline laboratory value, a minimum enrollment period. Being a healthcare-use variable is not sufficient for the bias, and these variables are the ones most likely to sit at the junction, because pre-baseline treatment decisions, incipient disease and the common causes of care-seeking and outcome all feed them. Nothing in the current workflow checks an eligibility definition for that structure before the analysis runs, and the reporting checklist asks what the criteria were rather than what conditioning on them does.

title: Eligibility criteria built from healthcare-use variables can induce selection through colliders
text:
Why it is open
Whether a criterion is a collider depends on the causal structure, which is what the study is trying to learn, so the check cannot be purely empirical. Observational data alone cannot certify the required structure: graph-learning algorithms recover a Markov equivalence class at best and are further limited by latent confounding, so they can flag candidates and never license removal. Removing a criterion also changes the target population, so the correction carries a cost that has to be argued clinically rather than statistically, and domain-grounded causal review therefore remains necessary rather than replaceable.

title: Eligibility criteria built from healthcare-use variables can induce selection through colliders
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Hernán MA, Robins JM. Using big data to emulate a target trial when a randomized trial is not available. Am J Epidemiol 2016;183(8):758-764
Requires eligibility to be specified as a trial would specify it, which is the discipline that makes the collider question askable at all.


Hansford HJ, Cashin AG, Jones MD, et al. Transparent reporting of observational studies emulating a target trial: the TARGET statement. JAMA 2025
Requires the eligibility criteria and their emulation to be reported, without requiring an assessment of the selection they induce.

title: Eligibility criteria built from healthcare-use variables can induce selection through colliders
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build a causal-discovery eligibility auditor that combines temporal checks with graph learning under explicit assumptions, flagging criteria that are post-baseline, that are colliders, or that encode healthcare use, and treat its output as advisory input to a domain review rather than as an automatic exclusion. Evaluate it on generated graphs with known structure, scoring collider-warning sensitivity, false-positive rate, expert agreement and, decisively, whether acting on the warnings reduces bias. Never let an algorithm define eligibility by maximizing the apparent treatment effect, which is a search over estimands dressed as a design step.

title: Eligibility criteria built from healthcare-use variables can induce selection through colliders
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “An eligibility criterion is a conditioning statement, and conditioning on a variable that is a common effect of treatment and outcome opens a path rather than closing one. Emulation protocols routinely build eligibility from healthcare-use variables such as a required prior visit, a recorded baseline laboratory value or a minimum enrollment period, all of which can be descendants of the treatment decision or of early disease. Nothing in the current workflow checks an eligibility definition for this property, and the reporting checklist asks what the criteria were rather than what conditioning on them does.”
What was wrong with it. The timing in the original was wrong. Eligibility is fixed before the time-zero treatment, so it cannot be a descendant of the treatment under study. The mechanism that does operate runs through pre-baseline treatment decisions, incipient disease and common causes of care-seeking and outcome, and it produces selection bias when the criterion is a collider or a descendant of one in the assumed graph. Being a healthcare-use variable is not by itself sufficient.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. The claim that nothing checks an eligibility definition for collider structure holds, and adjacent work is closer than the entry suggests. A 2026 npj Health Systems paper addresses eligibility-criteria-induced temporal selection directly, and machine-learning trial-eligibility emulation has been used to evaluate the generalizability of oncology trial results. A 2026 Frontiers in Medicine study uses emulation to evaluate eligibility criteria themselves in asthma and COPD. These evaluate the consequences of criteria rather than auditing them for collider structure before the analysis, which is what the entry proposes, so the specific artifact is still absent. Cites 10.1038/s44401-026-00082-3: Treats selection induced by eligibility criteria as the object of study, which is the mechanism the entry names.. Cites 10.3389/fmed.2026.1863026: Uses emulation to evaluate eligibility criteria, showing the criteria are becoming an object of analysis rather than a fixed input..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. Conditioning on an eligibility variable opens a noncausal path only when that variable is a collider, or a relevant descendant of one, in the assumed causal structure. Being a healthcare-use variable is not sufficient. The stated treatment-to-eligibility-to-outcome timing is also imprecise: eligibility fixed before time-zero treatment cannot be caused by that subsequent treatment or its subsequent outcome. The relevant graph may instead involve prebaseline treatment decisions, incipient disease, or common causes of treatment and outcome. Causal discovery does not universally return only a Markov equivalence class; what can be oriented depends on temporal, interventional, functional-form, and latent-confounding assumptions. It nevertheless cannot certify collider status from unrestricted observational data. An advisory tool for identifying possible temporal or collider problems remains an open development problem, but the asserted medium-high severity is context dependent rather than general.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. Inverted prior: treat collider-inducing eligibility as already audited in routine TTE workflows, then search for a method or tool that does so. Found conceptual and design literature, not a solution. Hernán and Robins (2016) already require that eligibility not use postbaseline events; that is design discipline, not an automated check of whether a healthcare-use criterion is a collider. Weiskopf et al. (2023, JAMIA) explicitly frame healthcare utilization as a common collider in EHR reuse and warn that conditioning on utilization (by selection or adjustment) opens non-causal paths; Digitale et al. (2023, J Clin Epidemiol) likewise describe collider-conditioning bias when restricting to people in care or with a disease history. Wang et al. (2026) restate that conditioning eligibility on utilization induces collider bias at cohort entry. These works strengthen that the mechanism is real; they do not supply a certified check. TARGET (Hansford et al., 2025) requires reporting of eligibility criteria and their emulation, not assessment of the selection graph those criteria induce; the entry’s reading of TARGET is accurate. Practical reviews (e.g., Tran et al., 2026) continue to document post-treatment eligibility as a frequent high-risk design error, which is evidence the gap is still live in applications. No retrieved paper or package implements a causal-discovery or temporal-rule eligibility auditor for proposed TTE criteria with evaluation on known graphs (sensitivity, false-positive rate, expert agreement, bias reduction when acting on warnings). Federated causal discovery and general DAG tools exist in adjacent literature but are not integrated into TTE protocol design or reporting checklists. Graph learning recovering only a Markov equivalence class under latent confounding remains a structural limit, as the entry states; formalizations of that limit do not close the problem. Queries run: collider + eligibility + target trial (2024–2026); healthcare utilization collider + eligibility; TARGET checklist collider/selection; causal discovery eligibility auditor TTE; CRAN/GitHub TrialEmulation, WeightIt, MatchIt, cobalt for eligibility-collider features (none found). Open as a workflow and tooling problem; prior art names the bias and forbids postbaseline criteria but does not solve systematic detection of healthcare-use colliders in eligibility definitions.

glm

open / supported. The claim is coherent and proportionate. It accurately describes how conditioning on healthcare-use variables for eligibility can induce collider bias. The reasons given for the problem being open are structurally sound: the causal structure is the target of inference, graph-learning algorithms can only flag candidates and cannot certify due to latent confounding, and removing a criterion changes the estimand. This is a claim about a real structural difficulty and current practice limitations, not an overstatement of impossibility.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-overstatement(n=1/4):codex
