title: No decomposition separates scientific-target mismatch from protocol compromise, mapping loss and estimation error
text: PRO-01 Overstated High priority Emerging Tractability 3/5

title: No decomposition separates scientific-target mismatch from protocol compromise, mapping loss and estimation error
text:
Statement
Three trials are in play in any emulation and only one is usually named: the ideal trial that would answer the decision-maker’s question, the target trial the investigator specifies, and the emulation the data support. Specifying the target trial closely around the available data conceals the distance between the first two, and the paper reports one estimate as though the chain were tight. What is missing is not an additive decomposition; that generally does not exist, because the transitions change populations, interventions, outcomes and scales, so the discrepancies do not add. What is missing is a documented lineage: the change from the decision question to the operational causal estimand, the assumptions mapping that estimand to an observed-data functional, and the estimation uncertainty, each recorded separately so a reader can see which step carries the load. No convention requires it, and no computable measure of the distance between two estimands is in use.

title: No decomposition separates scientific-target mismatch from protocol compromise, mapping loss and estimation error
text:
Why it is open
The first transition is a change of scientific question rather than a statistical error, so it has no sampling distribution and no natural metric. Measuring the distance between estimands requires a common space in which to compare an intervention that was never implementable with one that was, and that space has to be constructed rather than estimated. The incentives also run the wrong way: making the drift explicit weakens the paper’s claim without changing its number, so nothing but a reporting requirement would produce it.

title: No decomposition separates scientific-target mismatch from protocol compromise, mapping loss and estimation error
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Moreno-Betancur M, et al. The ideal trial: defining causal estimands that balance relevance and feasibility in target trial emulations and actual randomized trials. arXiv 2024
Distinguishes ideal, target and actual trials and argues that every discrepancy between them should be made explicit. It frames the problem and does not supply the decomposition.


Hernán MA, Robins JM. Using big data to emulate a target trial when a randomized trial is not available. Am J Epidemiol 2016;183(8):758-764
Establishes the target trial as the object to be specified, which is the middle term of the three and the only one the framework requires be written down.


Hansford HJ, et al. Design and implementation of observational studies emulating a target trial. JAMA Netw Open 2026
Design guidance for the operational steps, acknowledging that the operational methods remain scenario dependent.

title: No decomposition separates scientific-target mismatch from protocol compromise, mapping loss and estimation error
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Require an estimand lineage in the protocol, recording each transition as a change in population, treatment version, outcome definition or follow-up, written before the estimate exists. Report differences in intervention support and in target-population composition as concrete measures of drift, since both are computable from the data at hand and neither requires the ideal trial to be feasible. Publish the lineage next to the estimate, and state explicitly that it is a record of separate changes rather than an additive attribution of error.

title: No decomposition separates scientific-target mismatch from protocol compromise, mapping loss and estimation error
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Emulations should separately document changes from the decision question to the operational causal estimand, the assumptions mapping that estimand to an observed-data functional, and estimation uncertainty. This lineage need not form an additive numerical decomposition when populations, interventions, outcomes, or scales differ.
The source said. “Three trials are in play in any emulation and only one of them is usually named. There is the ideal trial that would answer the decision-maker’s question, the target trial that the investigator specifies, and the emulation the data actually support. Specifying the target trial closely around the available data conceals the distance between the first two, and the paper reports a single estimate as though the chain were tight. What does not exist is a decomposition of the total discrepancy into its four transitions: from the ideal estimand to the feasible target estimand, from that to the identified observed-data functional, and from that to the estimator’s output. Without one, a reader cannot tell whether a surprising result reflects estimation error or the fact that the question quietly changed at the first step.”
What was wrong with it. A decomposition in the arithmetic sense is not available and in general cannot be: when the populations, interventions, outcomes or scales differ across the transitions, the discrepancies do not add. What is achievable, and what the entry should have asked for, is a documented lineage recording each change separately rather than a single number attributed across four terms.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported-with-caveat): The framing is now published rather than a preprint: the ideal-trial paper the entry cites as arXiv 2405.10026 appeared in Epidemiology in 2026, and the entry should cite the journal version. A 2026 American Journal of Epidemiology paper sets out the anatomy of a causal estimand for population health research, which is the vocabulary a lineage would be written in. Neither supplies the decomposition the entry asks for: a formal accounting that attributes total discrepancy across the four transitions, with a computable measure of estimand distance. The claim survives with its citation corrected and its neighbors named.

Literature and prior-art check

A 2026 American Journal of Epidemiology paper sets out the anatomy of a causal estimand for population health research, which is the vocabulary a lineage would be written in. Neither supplies the decomposition the entry asks for: a formal accounting that attributes total discrepancy across the four transitions, with a computable measure of estimand distance. The claim survives with its citation corrected and its neighbors named. Cites 10.1097/ede.0000000000001933: The peer-reviewed version of the framing the entry cites as a preprint. The entry’s citation should move to this.. Cites 10.1093/aje/kwag079: Decomposes a causal estimand into its parts, which is the representation an estimand lineage would build on..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. A structured estimand lineage is a defensible reporting objective, but the proposed decomposition is not mathematically defined. The statement names four objects but enumerates only three transitions. Under valid identification, the observed-data functional equals the target causal estimand and is not a separate loss term. If identification assumptions fail, the resulting causal bias is generally not identified from the same data. Effects defined using different populations, interventions, outcomes, or scales also have no canonical additive distance. Differences in intervention support or population composition neither decompose nor necessarily bound the difference between effects without bridge and effect-heterogeneity assumptions. This is therefore an open reporting and formalization item, not a universally available decomposition whose absence prevents interpretation, and its asserted high severity is inflated.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. Inverted prior: searched for a formal four-step discrepancy decomposition (ideal→target→identified functional→estimator) in TTE. Own prior_work (Moreno-Betancur arXiv:2405.10026) frames ideal/target/actual trials and urges explicit discrepancies but does not supply a quantitative decomposition of total discrepancy into scientific-target mismatch, mapping loss, and estimation error. Hernán–Robins 2016 and Hansford 2026 are design/guidance, not decomposition. Searches for estimand lineage, estimand distance, and four-transition decomposition in AJE/Epidemiology/IJE/Sim/BMJ/JAMA and arXiv 2024–2026 returned framing and reporting proposals (ICH E9(R1), TARGET) but no operational metric or software that separates those four transitions. Still open as stated.

glm

open / overstated. The claim asserts that a decomposition ‘does not exist,’ which wears the language of impossibility. However, the reason given for it being open notes that the common space required for comparison ‘has to be constructed rather than estimated,’ implying that the decomposition is structurally possible but simply has not been developed or standardized in current practice. The claim is thus a statement about the current state of the field framed as an absolute.

R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2/4)

title: No decomposition separates scientific-target mismatch from protocol compromise, mapping loss and estimation error
text:
Related problems

title: Registrations record the final protocol and not the alternatives that were rejected
text: PRO-03 Confirmed open High priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: Registrations record the final protocol and not the alternatives that were rejected
text:
Statement
An emulation makes many defensible decisions: active comparator, washout period, time zero, grace period, how treatment episodes are constructed, censoring rules, follow-up length and outcome definition. Each has more than one reasonable answer, and the set of answers is the researcher’s degrees of freedom. Design guidance exists and states that the operational methods remain scenario dependent, so it narrows the set without closing it. Registrations record the specification that was finally run and not the alternatives considered, the order in which decisions were made, or which were revised after the data were inspected. A final protocol snapshot cannot reveal what was never logged, so a reader cannot distinguish a protocol written once from one converged upon, and no later audit can reconstruct it.

title: Registrations record the final protocol and not the alternatives that were rejected
text:
Why it is open
The information is destroyed rather than merely unreported: once a decision log is not kept there is no artifact to demand, and the investigators themselves cannot supply it. Registration systems were designed for randomized trials, where the protocol precedes the data, and have no natural slot for a design developed against an existing dataset. Requiring a full multiverse imposes a cost proportional to the number of decisions, which for a longitudinal emulation is large, so the honest practice is also the expensive one.

title: Registrations record the final protocol and not the alternatives that were rejected

Work

Hansford HJ, et al. Design and implementation of observational studies emulating a target trial. JAMA Netw Open 2026

Hansford HJ, Cashin AG, Jones MD, et al. Transparent reporting of observational studies emulating a target trial: the TARGET statement. JAMA 2025

title: Registrations record the final protocol and not the alternatives that were rejected
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Require prospective versioning, dated amendment and decision logs, and trusted timestamps, so the chronology is auditable rather than remembered; nothing added after the fact substitutes for this. Prespecify a primary emulation plus a principled design multiverse over the decisions known to move estimates, and keep the distinct estimands explicit when reporting the spread rather than pooling specifications that answer different questions. Hash the executable specification before outcome analysis, which makes prespecification checkable by a third party instead of taken on trust.

title: Registrations record the final protocol and not the alternatives that were rejected
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “An emulation makes many defensible decisions: active comparator, washout period, time zero, grace period, how treatment episodes are constructed, censoring rules, follow-up length and outcome definition. Each has more than one reasonable answer, and the set of answers is the researcher’s degrees of freedom. Registrations, where they exist, record only the specification that was finally run; they do not record the alternatives considered, the order in which decisions were made, or which decisions were revised after the data were inspected. A reader therefore cannot distinguish a protocol written once from one converged upon.”
What was wrong with it. No auditor found the claim overstated. The proposed direction is sharpened: a protocol snapshot cannot reveal revisions that were never logged, so the requirement is prospective versioning with trusted timestamps rather than fuller reporting after the fact, and a specification sensitivity analysis has to keep the distinct estimands explicit rather than pooling them.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): Nothing in the corpus records a decision log, a dated chronology of design choices, or the alternatives rejected during protocol development. Quality-assessment tools for observational comparative effectiveness studies, and comprehensive analyses of emulation practice in oncology, evaluate the specification that was published rather than the process that produced it. The entry’s claim is about an artifact nobody keeps, which is consistent with its absence from a literature search: the evidence for it is the absence of any paper reporting one.

Prospective version control, amendment records, decision logs, and trusted timestamps can preserve the history directly. The categorical assertion that registrations retain only the final protocol is not established by technical reasoning, and an unlogged history is unavailable to an auditor but not necessarily destroyed. A full multiverse is neither required for provenance nor automatically interpretable: changing populations, comparators, strategies, or outcomes creates different estimands, so their estimates do not constitute an uncertainty distribution for one parameter. A hash establishes integrity only when paired with a trusted timestamp and does not prove that no alternative analysis existed. This is a roadmap and reporting-standard item rather than a high-severity statistical gap.

The reason given—that registration systems were designed for randomized trials where the protocol precedes the data and have no natural slot for a design developed against an existing dataset—directly entails that the artifact required to settle the issue is not currently produced or demanded by these systems.

title: Emulation is proposed for non-pharmaceutical and policy interventions whose treatment versions and assignment units are not defined
text: PRO-05 Partially addressed Medium-high priority Emerging Tractability 3/5

title: Emulation is proposed for non-pharmaceutical and policy interventions whose treatment versions and assignment units are not defined
text:
Statement
Interference, combination therapies, multiple treatment versions and non-pharmaceutical interventions all strain the two-arm, individually assigned, well-defined-intervention assumptions the standard emulation protocol makes. Policy interventions are the sharpest case: delivered to a place or an organization rather than a person, varying in content by implementer, arriving gradually rather than on a date, and often with no comparable version of not receiving them. A policy emulation therefore has to specify the assignment unit, the timing, the comparator, the intervention versions or a stochastic rule over them, the exposure mapping under interference, and a cluster-level estimand. Emulation is being applied to such questions with these filled in by analogy, and when treatment varies only across jurisdictions the causal information comes from the number of independent jurisdictions and the variation in adoption, not from the patient count.

title: Emulation is proposed for non-pharmaceutical and policy interventions whose treatment versions and assignment units are not defined
text:
Why it is open
A well-defined intervention is a requirement of the causal framework rather than of emulation specifically, so this is inherited rather than introduced and the emulation literature has no special claim on solving it. Version variation is intrinsic to implementation rather than incidental, so consistency fails by construction rather than by accident. And the quantity that actually limits inference, independent jurisdictions with variation in adoption, is usually small and cannot be increased by adding patients, which is the resource these studies have.

title: Emulation is proposed for non-pharmaceutical and policy interventions whose treatment versions and assignment units are not defined
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Papadogeorgou G, Mealli F, Zigler CM. Causal inference with interfering units for cluster and population level treatment allocation programs. Biometrics 2019;75(3):778-787
Provides the estimand framework for cluster and population-level allocation, which is the setting a policy emulation is in whether or not it says so.


Hernán MA, Robins JM. Using big data to emulate a target trial when a randomized trial is not available. Am J Epidemiol 2016;183(8):758-764
States the well-defined-intervention requirement that policy questions strain, and the protocol components a policy emulation has to fill.

title: Emulation is proposed for non-pharmaceutical and policy interventions whose treatment versions and assignment units are not defined
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Write protocol templates for cluster and policy target trials in which the assignment unit, the exposure mapping, the treatment-version class or stochastic version rule, and the cluster-level estimand are explicit components rather than assumptions. Where versions cannot be unified, define the estimand over the observed distribution of versions and say so, rather than naming an intervention no jurisdiction implemented. Report the number of independent jurisdictions and the variation in adoption as the design’s effective information, alongside the patient count rather than behind it.

title: Emulation is proposed for non-pharmaceutical and policy interventions whose treatment versions and assignment units are not defined
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Interference, combination therapies, multiple treatment versions and non-pharmaceutical interventions all violate the two-arm, individually assigned, well-defined-intervention assumptions that the standard emulation protocol makes. Non-pharmaceutical and policy interventions are the sharpest case: the intervention is delivered to a place or an organization rather than a person, its content varies by implementer, its timing is gradual rather than dated, and there is often no version of not receiving it that is comparable. Emulation is nonetheless being applied to such questions, with the protocol components filled in by analogy. What is missing is a statement of which protocol components a policy intervention can actually satisfy and what estimand results when several cannot.”
What was wrong with it. The entry counted jurisdictions as the unit that limits inference. The sharper statement is that when treatment varies only across jurisdictions, the causal information is carried by the number of independent jurisdictions and by the variation in adoption, not by the patient count and not by jurisdiction count alone.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): The corpus contains policy and service-level emulations, including chronic disease management programs and national incentive schemes evaluated with the target trial approach, and contains no protocol template stating which components a policy intervention can satisfy or what estimand results when several cannot. A 2026 substance-use workshop proceedings discusses methodological innovation for emulation in that setting, which is the nearest thing to the templates the entry asks for. The claim that policy emulations are published with individual-level precision and jurisdiction-level information is supported by the applied papers in the corpus rather than by a methodological source, which is why the confidence is moderate. codex dissented (overstated): Target trial emulation is not intrinsically restricted to two arms or individual assignment. Combination therapies can be defined as multicomponent strategies; policies can be assigned at cluster level; and interference can be handled through explicit exposure mappings and cluster or population-level estimands. Multiple versions do not make consistency fail by construction when versions are specified, shown irrelevant, or incorporated into a well-defined stochastic intervention. The defect arises when a vague treatment label, assignment unit, version rule, timing, or interference structure is left unspecified. Cluster-level treatment variation makes the number and adoption patterns of independent clusters central to precision, but the effective sample size is not literally always the number of jurisdictions, and no universal minimum count is defensible without the design, dependence structure, and inferential method. Averaging over an observed version distribution is causal only after that stochastic intervention and its identification assumptions are defined. The cited cluster-allocation framework already resolves the alleged absence of an estimand framework, while standardized emulation protocols and finite-cluster guidance remain open.

Literature and prior-art check

The claim that policy emulations are published with individual-level precision and jurisdiction-level information is supported by the applied papers in the corpus rather than by a methodological source, which is why the confidence is moderate. Cites 10.1016/j.josat.2026.210065: Addresses emulation in a service and policy setting where the intervention is delivered at more than the individual level..

Combination therapies can be defined as multicomponent strategies; policies can be assigned at cluster level; and interference can be handled through explicit exposure mappings and cluster or population-level estimands. Averaging over an observed version distribution is causal only after that stochastic intervention and its identification assumptions are defined. The cited cluster-allocation framework already resolves the alleged absence of an estimand framework, while standardized emulation protocols and finite-cluster guidance remain open. Cites 10.1111/biom.13049: As characterized in the supplied record, it provides estimands for cluster and population-level allocation under interference, resolving the claim that these settings inherently lack a causal estimand framework. It does not by itself supply a target-trial protocol template or solve finite-cluster inference..

Grok 4.5, recency lens

Policy and NPI emulations appear increasingly, sometimes with cluster assignment made explicit. Still missing: standard protocol templates stating which seven components a policy/NPI can satisfy, estimands over observed version distributions when versions cannot be unified, and minimum jurisdiction-unit counts for credible assignment-level inference. Partial prior art on identification; gap on TTE protocol templates and unit-count guidance remains open. Cites 10.1111/biom.13049: Partial: estimand framework for cluster and population-level allocation with interference; does not supply TTE protocol templates for policy/NPI, version-distribution estimands as default reporting, or minimum jurisdiction-level sample-size rules..

It identifies a gap in applying emulation to non-pharmaceutical and policy interventions where treatment versions and assignment units are not well-defined. title: There is no assumption dashboard, so diagnosable and undiagnosable assumptions are reported alike
text: REG-02 Confirmed open High priority Promising Tractability 5/5

title: There is no assumption dashboard, so diagnosable and undiagnosable assumptions are reported alike
text:
Statement
Exchangeability and consistency cannot be established from observed data. Neither, strictly, can positivity, model correctness or phenotype validity: the available checks reveal or falsify particular problems and certify none of them. Current reports blur both distinctions. A propensity-score overlap plot is offered and the reader infers that the assumptions have been checked, when the plot is a partial diagnostic of one of them and silent on the rest. No standard panel exists, so what appears varies by author and by journal, and an absent diagnostic cannot be distinguished from one that was run and not reported. A single panel cannot be adequate for every design, which is a constraint on the solution rather than an argument against it.

title: There is no assumption dashboard, so diagnosable and undiagnosable assumptions are reported alike
text:
Why it is open
A reporting panel is a convention rather than a discovery, and conventions need an adopting body. Several components are not standardized as measurements: longitudinal balance and support by treatment history have no agreed summary statistic, and no single summary suits every design, so the panel has to be a family indexed by design rather than a fixed list. Separating what is diagnosable from what is not also makes the undiagnosable assumptions conspicuous, which is uncomfortable and is the point.

title: There is no assumption dashboard, so diagnosable and undiagnosable assumptions are reported alike
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Hansford HJ, Cashin AG, Jones MD, et al. Transparent reporting of observational studies emulating a target trial: the TARGET statement. JAMA 2025
Establishes what must be reported about the protocol and its emulation, and is explicitly not a risk-of-bias or diagnostic standard.


Hansford HJ, et al. Reporting of observational studies explicitly aiming to emulate randomized trials: a systematic review. JAMA Netw Open 2023
Across 200 published emulations, 43% did not describe all key emulation components and 57% did not describe both the target protocol and its emulation, which is the measured baseline of reporting practice.

title: There is no assumption dashboard, so diagnosable and undiagnosable assumptions are reported alike
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Define a reporting panel that separates causal assumptions the data cannot establish from partial diagnostics of empirical support, nuisance-model performance, balance, weighting, censoring, missingness and measurement validity, and state for each diagnostic what it can falsify rather than what it confirms. Standardize summary statistics for longitudinal balance and support by history, the two components with no agreed form, and index the panel by design rather than fixing one list. Pair it with the reporting checklist so a missing panel is a visible omission rather than an inference.

title: There is no assumption dashboard, so diagnosable and undiagnosable assumptions are reported alike
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Exchangeability and consistency cannot be established from the observed data. Positivity, model behavior, balance and measurement validity can at least be diagnosed. Current reports blur the distinction: a propensity-score overlap plot is offered, and the reader is left to infer that the assumptions have been checked, when the plot bears on one of them and is silent on the rest. No standard set of diagnostics exists for an emulation, so what appears varies by author and by journal, and the absence of a diagnostic cannot be distinguished from a diagnostic that was run and not reported.”
What was wrong with it. The entry drew the line in the wrong place. Positivity, model correctness and phenotype validity are not simply diagnosable: the available checks reveal or falsify particular problems and certify none of them, so the honest division is between assumptions the data cannot establish and partial diagnostics of empirical support. No single longitudinal summary is adequate for every design either, which limits what a standard panel can be.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): No assumption dashboard appears in the corpus. Methodological quality assessment tools for observational comparative effectiveness studies exist and score reported design features rather than requiring a standard diagnostic panel, and none separates empirically testable diagnostics from untestable assumptions in its output. The entry’s claim that a missing diagnostic cannot be distinguished from an unreported one follows from the absence of a required panel and is supported by the reporting review showing that 43% of 200 emulations did not describe all key components.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. No assumption dashboard appears in the corpus. Methodological quality assessment tools for observational comparative effectiveness studies exist and score reported design features rather than requiring a standard diagnostic panel, and none separates empirically testable diagnostics from untestable assumptions in its output. The entry’s claim that a missing diagnostic cannot be distinguished from an unreported one follows from the absence of a required panel and is supported by the reporting review showing that 43% of 200 emulations did not describe all key components. Cites 10.1016/s1473-3099(26)00058-7: An appraisal instrument in this space, which scores what was reported rather than requiring a diagnostic panel.. Cites 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.36023: Measures how incompletely emulations report their components, which is the baseline the entry’s claim rests on..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. A standardized reporting convention remains a legitimate open implementation issue, but the proposed testable versus untestable division is too coarse. Observed data cannot establish exchangeability or consistency. Empirical positivity problems, nuisance-model behavior, and measured-covariate balance can be investigated, but finite-sample diagnostics cannot establish population positivity or model correctness. Measurement validity normally requires labeled, replicated, or external validation data, and balance is a property of the fitted analysis rather than a causal assumption. A dashboard would improve transparency but would not certify identification, so this is a reporting roadmap item rather than a solution to a decision-critical methodological gap.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. No adopted, author-facing assumption dashboard that separates diagnosable diagnostics from undiagnosable identifying assumptions for target trial emulations was found. TARGET (Hansford/Cashin et al., JAMA 2025; also BMJ co-publication) is a 21-item reporting guideline for observational studies that explicitly emulate a target trial: it requires statement of the target protocol, mapping to data, identifying assumptions, and sensitivity analyses. It is deliberately not a risk-of-bias tool and not a standardized diagnostic panel; its own positioning matches the report’s prior-work note. Hansford et al. JAMA Netw Open 2023 documents uneven reporting of emulation components, which is baseline practice, not a dashboard. ROBINS-I and ROBINS-I V2 (launch materials 2024) structure reviewer risk-of-bias judgments relative to a specified target trial; that is systematic-review assessment, not a publication convention that forces authors to display balance over time, weight tails, effective sample size, support by treatment history, phenotype validity, and sensitivity contours in a fixed layout with testable panels visually separated from exchangeability and consistency. STaRT-RWE and HARPER improve protocol prespecification and reproducibility; they do not standardize longitudinal diagnostic summaries. Software ecosystems (cobalt, WeightIt, MatchIt, ipw, gfoRmula, lmtp, ltmle, adjustedCurves) supply balance, overlap, and weight diagnostics for specific designs, including some longitudinal use, but there is no field-wide agreed summary statistic for longitudinal balance or support-by-history, and no journal or regulator-mandated dashboard that makes omission of a panel a visible reporting failure. Method papers that propose or apply QBA, negative controls, or multi-panel diagnostics remain proposals or local practice, not an adopting-body convention. The core structural claim remains: conventions require adoption, and none has closed the reported gap. Queries included: assumption/diagnostic dashboard target trial; TARGET as diagnostic standard; longitudinal balance standardization cobalt WeightIt; ROBINS-I TTE diagnostics; STaRT-RWE HARPER assumption reporting 2024–2026; arXiv/medRxiv causal diagnostic checklist.

glm

abstain / supported. The claim is coherent and proportionate. It identifies a real gap in current reporting practice (no standard dashboard) and the rationale correctly identifies the structural reasons (lack of standardized measurements for longitudinal balance, need for an adopting body). This is a claim about current practice. I abstain on the status axis because verifying the current state of reporting practice requires evidence I cannot reach.

Decision path

title: Sequential emulation creates repeated participation and calendar-time confounding that its efficiency gain conceals
text: SEQ-01 Overstated High priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: Sequential emulation creates repeated participation and calendar-time confounding that its efficiency gain conceals
text:
Statement
Sequential emulation exploits repeated eligibility: a new trial is emulated at each decision point, and a person eligible at many points contributes to many of them. The resulting within-person dependence has been addressed: clustering by person, and confidence-interval procedures for survival outcomes compared across the sandwich estimator, nonparametric bootstrap, jackknife and a linearized estimating function bootstrap, which covers better in the small-sample, low-event-rate regime that motivates the design. What has not been addressed is the calendar-time structure. Trials begun at different times occur under different treatment availability, guidelines and background risk, so a pooled estimate assumes an effect common to start times that differ in all three. Trial start is not conventionally modeled flexibly, treatment-by-start-time heterogeneity is not conventionally examined, and trial-specific estimates are not reported alongside the pooled one, so a pooled effect resting on incompatible starts is invisible.

title: Sequential emulation creates repeated participation and calendar-time confounding that its efficiency gain conceals
text:
Why it is open
Testing the common-effect assumption costs the efficiency the design was adopted for, since trial-specific estimates are individually imprecise by construction. A person’s later eligibility is itself a consequence of earlier untreated survival, so the trials are linked causally rather than only statistically, and whether that is innocuous depends on the outcome model being correct, which is the thing under test. Reporting per-start estimates also complicates a paper whose selling point was a single efficient number.

title: Sequential emulation creates repeated participation and calendar-time confounding that its efficiency gain conceals
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Caniglia EC, et al. Emulating target trials to avoid immortal time bias: an application to antibiotic initiation. Epidemiology 2023
A worked sequential emulation showing how repeated decision points remove immortal time bias where treatment can begin at many times.


Inference procedures in sequential trial emulation with survival outcomes: comparing confidence intervals based on the sandwich variance estimator, bootstrap and jackknife. Stat Methods Med Res 2025
Compares four variance procedures for sequential trial emulation and recommends the linearized estimating function bootstrap in the regime that motivates the design.


Causal inference in survival analysis using longitudinal observational data: sequential trials and marginal structural models. Stat Med 2023
Sets out the sequential-trials estimator alongside marginal structural models for survival outcomes.


Su L, et al. TrialEmulation: an R package to emulate target trials for causal analysis of observational time-to-event data. arXiv 2024
Implements the sequence expansion and censoring weights the design requires.

title: Sequential emulation creates repeated participation and calendar-time confounding that its efficiency gain conceals
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Model trial start flexibly rather than adjusting it away, examine treatment-by-start-time heterogeneity, and report trial-specific estimates alongside the pooled one, so a pooled effect resting on incompatible start times is visible. Cluster by person as standard, and use a person-level bootstrap where uncertainty from the estimated weights is material rather than assuming the sandwich estimator suffices. Establish whether the efficiency gain survives the correct variance treatment, since the case for the design has usually been made under the naive variance.

title: Sequential emulation creates repeated participation and calendar-time confounding that its efficiency gain conceals
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Pooling across sequentially emulated trials assumes an effect common to start times that differ in treatment availability, guidelines and background risk, and trial-specific estimates are not conventionally reported alongside the pooled one.
The source said. “Sequential emulation exploits repeated eligibility: a new trial is emulated at each decision point, and a person who is eligible at many points contributes to many trials. This uses the data better than a single baseline emulation and it introduces three complications together. The same person appears in many nested trials, so the observations are dependent in a way the pooled analysis must handle. Trials begun at different calendar times occur under different treatment availability, guidelines and background risk, so calendar time confounds the pooled contrast unless it is modeled. And a person’s later eligibility is itself a consequence of earlier untreated survival, which links the trials causally rather than merely statistically. The efficiency gain is real and it is what makes these complications easy to overlook.”
What was wrong with it. The variance half of the claim is answered. Confidence-interval procedures for sequential trial emulation with survival outcomes have been compared across the sandwich estimator, nonparametric bootstrap, jackknife and a linearized estimating function bootstrap, with the last recommended in the small-sample, low-event-rate regime that motivates the design. The entry asked for that work as though it had not been done. What survives is the calendar-time half and the reporting practice.
Dissent. grok dissented (supported-with-caveat): Inverted-prior search finds substantial 2024–2025 work on two of the three complications the entry bundles, so the problem is not open as a blank slate. On repeated participation and design-induced dependence, Limozin, Seaman and Su (arXiv 2407.08317; Stat Methods Med Res 2025) run a dedicated simulation comparing sandwich, nonparametric bootstrap, linearised estimating-function bootstrap and jackknife CIs for marginal risk differences under sequential trial emulation (STE), explicitly because the same patient can enter many nested trials. They report that sandwich/bootstrap/jackknife can account for that correlation, that sandwich is conservative when weight uncertainty is ignored, and that LEF bootstrap has the best small/moderate-sample coverage. That is exactly the variance and person-level bootstrap coverage work the agenda’s “direction” asks for; TrialEmulation is the implementation vehicle they use. On calendar-time confounding of pooled contrasts, DeMonte, Shook-Sa and Hudgens (arXiv 2403.18115) formalize nested trial emulation when the effect is allowed to vary over calendar time and/or time since treatment, provide a trial-effect-homogeneity test, and estimate trial-specific as well as calendar-time-varying vaccine effectiveness. That is the “model calendar time as effect modifier and report trial-specific estimates alongside the pooled one” program, at least in the vaccine setting where calendar-time heterogeneity is most obvious. Keogh et al. (Stat Med 2023) already recommended formal tests of trial-by-covariate interactions and compared sequential-trial efficiency to MSM-IPTW. What remains open, and why this is only partial: (1) Limozin evaluates CI coverage and computation, not a definitive redesign verdict that the efficiency case for STE survives person-clustered variance in general applications; sandwich conservatism means naive SEs can still overstate precision relative to person-level resampling. (2) DeMonte’s calendar-time-varying MSMs are developed and simulated for nested vaccine trials; they do not close the problem for arbitrary sustained pharmacoepidemiologic strategies or for routine non-VE sequential emulations that still pool under a common-effect assumption. (3) The third arm (later eligibility as a consequence of earlier untreated survival, so that trials are causally linked and the selection process depends on the outcome model being correct) is not resolved by either paper; no 2024–2026 work found identifies that selection away or shows it is innocuous under weak conditions. Package activity (TrialEmulation, SEQTaRget on CRAN) implements expansion and weighting but does not by itself close the identification/inference gaps. Cited prior work (Caniglia 2023; Su arXiv 2402.12083) illustrates and software-izes the design rather than solving the three complications. Queries that returned no full solution: “sequential trial emulation selection later eligibility untreated survival”; “efficiency gain sequential nested trial person-cluster sandwich vs naive”; general-journal 2024–2026 searches for a single paper closing all three arms together. Net: variance and calendar-time arms are partially methodologically addressed with evaluated tools; the bundled “still open and easy to overlook” framing is still useful but overstates residual openness if it ignores Limozin 2025 and DeMonte 2024.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The entry asks for variance estimators that account for repeated participation across nested trials and for a check of their coverage against a bootstrap over persons. That work has been done. A 2025 Statistical Methods in Medical Research paper compares confidence intervals for sequential trial emulation with survival outcomes across the sandwich variance estimator, nonparametric bootstrap, jackknife and a linearized estimating function bootstrap, and finds the last has better coverage in the small-sample, low-event-rate, low-treatment-prevalence regime that motivates the design. Sequential trials and marginal structural models were compared for survival outcomes in 2023. The dependence half of the entry is therefore substantially answered and should not be published as open. The calendar-time half, that pooling across start times assumes a common effect and that trial-specific estimates are not reported, is untouched by this work and survives. Cites 10.1177/09622802251356594: Directly supplies and evaluates variance estimation for sequential trial emulation, including a computationally feasible bootstrap alternative, which is what the entry asks for as future work.. Cites 10.1002/sim.9718: Sets out the sequential-trials estimator alongside marginal structural models for survival outcomes, establishing the analysis the entry describes..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. Repeated eligibility does create within-person dependence, but the pinned implementation already addresses the standard version of that problem: TrialEmulation clusters its sandwich covariance by the original person identifier. It also includes trial start period in the pooled outcome model by default and accepts user-specified trial-period formulas, including interactions for effect heterogeneity. Calendar time confounds a pooled person-trial contrast only when it predicts both treatment and outcome; treatment-effect variation across start times is a separate effect-modification issue. Likewise, only a pooled model constrained to one treatment coefficient assumes a common effect. Later eligibility changes the eligible survivor population, but this is part of the sequence of trial-specific protocols and does not make validity depend specifically on outcome-model correctness. The efficiency gain is also not guaranteed after accounting for correlation and variable weights. Remaining work concerns coverage when weights are estimated, finite-sample behavior, diagnostics for treatment-by-start-time heterogeneity, and clearly defined standardization across changing eligible populations. Those are legitimate methodological and reporting questions, but they do not support the asserted high-severity claim that basic variance and calendar-time methods are missing. Cites CRAN TrialEmulation 0.0.4.11: Confirms that the pinned package exports the sequential expansion and pooled marginal structural model interfaces.. Cites CRAN TrialEmulation 0.0.4.11: The pooled marginal structural model includes trial start period by default and exposes the term for flexible specification.. Cites CRAN TrialEmulation 0.0.4.11: Implements person-clustered sandwich covariance, directly addressing dependence from repeated participation..

Grok 4.5, recency lens

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Inverted-prior search finds substantial 2024–2025 work on two of the three complications the entry bundles, so the problem is not open as a blank slate. On repeated participation and design-induced dependence, Limozin, Seaman and Su (arXiv 2407.08317; Stat Methods Med Res 2025) run a dedicated simulation comparing sandwich, nonparametric bootstrap, linearised estimating-function bootstrap and jackknife CIs for marginal risk differences under sequential trial emulation (STE), explicitly because the same patient can enter many nested trials. They report that sandwich/bootstrap/jackknife can account for that correlation, that sandwich is conservative when weight uncertainty is ignored, and that LEF bootstrap has the best small/moderate-sample coverage. That is exactly the variance and person-level bootstrap coverage work the agenda’s “direction” asks for; TrialEmulation is the implementation vehicle they use. On calendar-time confounding of pooled contrasts, DeMonte, Shook-Sa and Hudgens (arXiv 2403.18115) formalize nested trial emulation when the effect is allowed to vary over calendar time and/or time since treatment, provide a trial-effect-homogeneity test, and estimate trial-specific as well as calendar-time-varying vaccine effectiveness. That is the “model calendar time as effect modifier and report trial-specific estimates alongside the pooled one” program, at least in the vaccine setting where calendar-time heterogeneity is most obvious. Keogh et al. (Stat Med 2023) already recommended formal tests of trial-by-covariate interactions and compared sequential-trial efficiency to MSM-IPTW. (2) DeMonte’s calendar-time-varying MSMs are developed and simulated for nested vaccine trials; they do not close the problem for arbitrary sustained pharmacoepidemiologic strategies or for routine non-VE sequential emulations that still pool under a common-effect assumption. (3) The third arm (later eligibility as a consequence of earlier untreated survival, so that trials are causally linked and the selection process depends on the outcome model being correct) is not resolved by either paper; no 2024–2026 work found identifies that selection away or shows it is innocuous under weak conditions. Package activity (TrialEmulation, SEQTaRget on CRAN) implements expansion and weighting but does not by itself close the identification/inference gaps. Cited prior work (Caniglia 2023; Su arXiv 2402.12083) illustrates and software-izes the design rather than solving the three complications. Queries that returned no full solution: “sequential trial emulation selection later eligibility untreated survival”; “efficiency gain sequential nested trial person-cluster sandwich vs naive”; general-journal 2024–2026 searches for a single paper closing all three arms together. Net: variance and calendar-time arms are partially methodologically addressed with evaluated tools; the bundled “still open and easy to overlook” framing is still useful but overstates residual openness if it ignores Limozin 2025 and DeMonte 2024. Cites arxiv:2407.08317: Derives and simulates person-level sandwich, nonparametric bootstrap, LEF bootstrap and jackknife inference for STE marginal risk differences when the same individual contributes to multiple nested trials; gives practical guidance on which CI method has near-nominal coverage by sample size, event rate and treatment prevalence. Partially closes the repeated-participation variance arm and the agenda’s call to check coverage against bootstrap over persons.. Cites doi:10.1177/09622802251356594: Peer-reviewed Statistical Methods in Medical Research version of the same STE variance comparison (PubMed 40631395); same resolving role as arXiv:2407.08317 for the dependence/variance complication.. Cites arxiv:2403.18115: Provides NTE IPW estimators and MSMs that allow the effect to vary over calendar time and/or time since treatment, plus a formal test of trial effect homogeneity; estimates trial-specific and calendar-time-varying effects rather than only a pooled common effect. Partially closes the calendar-time confounding / pooled-contrast arm for nested trials (vaccine effectiveness setting)..

glm

open / supported. The claim is internally consistent and proportionate. It identifies three genuine complications of sequential target trial emulation—design-induced dependence from repeated participation, calendar-time confounding across start times, and survival-conditioned later eligibility—and frames them as overlooked rather than impossible to address. The reasoning for openness is coherent: pooling requires a common-effect assumption that calendar-time variation challenges; the dependence has no natural clustering variable beyond the person; and the selection process depends on outcome-model correctness, which is the inferential target. None of these are asserted as structural impossibilities; they are framed as current-practice gaps, which is the correct register. The proposed directions (model calendar time as effect modifier, derive person-level variance estimators, compare efficiency under correct variance) are constructive and imply the problems are solvable, reinforcing that the claim is about practice rather than principle. The scope is appropriate: the claim does not say sequential emulation should be abandoned, only that its efficiency gain conceals complications that need methodological attention. The severity is proportionate to the cost of a wrong pooled estimate in a treatment-effect decision. I cannot verify whether specific software or recent papers already resolve all three complications together, so I do not downgrade from open, but the claim as stated does not depend on any software capability assertion.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=3/4) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2/4)

title: Generative models are evaluated on distributional fidelity and used for causal work
text: SFW-02 Partially addressed Medium-high priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: Generative models are evaluated on distributional fidelity and used for causal work
text:
Statement
Generative patient models would support privacy-preserving code development, power planning and method stress testing, and synthetic patient data have shown value as a benchmark environment. The evaluation does not match the use. Marginal and temporal fidelity do not validate a generator’s counterfactual behavior, and cannot: without identifying assumptions or interventional ground truth, two generators indistinguishable on observed data can disagree on some interventions. A model optimized for fidelity can therefore reproduce every observed association while generating wrong counterfactuals, wrong overlap and wrong time ordering, because none of those appears in the loss. Privacy mechanisms compound it by suppressing rare patterns, which are often the causally important ones. Synthetic data are not evidence about treatment effects unless the generating model is causally valid, and current benchmarks do not test whether it is.

title: Generative models are evaluated on distributional fidelity and used for causal work
text:
Why it is open
Causal fidelity is not identifiable from the observational data the generator was trained on, which is the same reason the analyses these data are meant to support need assumptions. Evaluating it therefore requires a gold-standard structural model or external interventional evidence rather than a real dataset, which changes what is being validated. Privacy and causal fidelity are also in direct tension, since the mechanisms that protect rare individuals remove the rare strata that carry the overlap.

title: Generative models are evaluated on distributional fidelity and used for causal work
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Shi, et al. Generating high-fidelity privacy-conscious synthetic patient data for causal effect estimation with multiple treatments. Front Artif Intell 2022
Builds synthetic patient generation aimed specifically at causal effect estimation with multiple treatments, which is where the fidelity question becomes sharp.

title: Generative models are evaluated on distributional fidelity and used for causal work
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build causal benchmarks on an explicit structural data-generating model with known counterfactuals, or on external interventional evidence, rather than on a real dataset the generator can be scored against. Assess conditional support, longitudinal ordering, effect fidelity and privacy loss separately, since a single score lets a model trade one against another invisibly. State as a standing rule that synthetic-effect estimates are not clinical evidence, and confine synthetic data to code development, power planning and method benchmarking.

title: Generative models are evaluated on distributional fidelity and used for causal work
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Generative patient models would support privacy-preserving code development, power planning and method stress testing, and synthetic patient data have shown value as a benchmark environment. The evaluation practice does not match the use. A model optimized for marginal or temporal fidelity can reproduce every observed association while generating wrong counterfactuals, wrong overlap and wrong time ordering, because none of those quantities appears in the loss. Privacy mechanisms compound this by suppressing rare patterns, and rare patterns are often exactly the causally important ones. Synthetic data are not evidence about treatment effects unless the generating model is causally valid, and current benchmarks do not test whether it is.”
What was wrong with it. Sharpened rather than corrected: the reason marginal fidelity does not validate a generator is that without identifying assumptions or interventional ground truth, observationally indistinguishable generators can disagree on some interventions, which is why a causal benchmark needs an explicit structural model or external interventional evidence rather than a better fidelity metric.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): The corpus contains synthetic patient generation aimed at causal effect estimation and generative approaches to causal graphs, and contains no evaluation of a generative model against a known structural model’s interventional distributions. The entry’s claim, that fidelity evaluation does not test causal validity, is consistent with the absence, and the confidence is capped because the generative-model literature sits mostly in venues these eight phrases would not retrieve. grok dissented (supported): Inverted prior: assume causal evaluation of synthetic patients is already standard. The report’s own prior work (Shi et al. 2022) already builds privacy-conscious synthetic data with ground-truth multi-treatment effects, so the agenda’s proposed direction (causally annotated synthetic trials) has a published instance rather than a blank slate. Amad et al. (arXiv 2510.18768; NeurIPS 2025) explicitly diagnose evaluation on distributional resemblance while treatments invite causal analysis, state desiderata (covariate distribution, treatment assignment mechanism, outcome generation mechanism), propose metrics (precision/recall on covariates, propensity JSD, PEHE utility), and introduce STEAM to factor generation along that DGP. That is substantive prior art on evaluation design and generation, not mere marginal fidelity.
It does not solve the problem as a field practice claim. STEAM and Shi are proposals/datasets, not industry standard. Causal fidelity of a generator trained only on observational data remains non-identifiable without a structural gold standard; two SCMs can match all observational margins and disagree on interventions. Privacy mechanisms that erase rare strata still conflict with positivity-relevant tails. Hernandez et al. (Front Digit Health 2025) still frame synthetic tabular evaluation around fidelity/utility/privacy without interventional ground truth. Queries run: causal fidelity synthetic evaluation; STEAM treatment effect synthetic data; Shi 2022 ground truth; PEHE synthetic medical; synthetic patient counterfactual evaluation 2024–2026. No evidence that clinical or regulatory use treats synthetic-effect estimates as non-evidence by default, nor that mainstream generators are scored on intervention response error. Partial solve of evaluation methodology; the practice mismatch remains open.

Cites 10.3389/frai.2022.918813: Provides a large synthetic patient resource with explicit ground-truth effects for many hypertension treatments, showing that causally annotated synthetic data for multi-treatment effect estimation already exists as prior art (partial instance of the agenda’s proposed direction).. open / supported. The claim is structurally sound and proportionate. The core identifiability argument—that two structural models agreeing on every observational distribution can disagree on every interventional one—is a well-established result in causal inference and correctly grounds the claim that causal fidelity cannot be assessed from observational data alone. The claim does not assert that causally valid generators are impossible to build; it asserts that current benchmarks do not test for causal validity, which is a claim about practice, not about impossibility. The standing rule proposed—that synthetic-effect estimates are not clinical evidence—is proportionate to the severity of the error (clinical decisions based on non-causally-valid synthetic data). The scope is right: the claim is about evaluation practice, not about the existence of generative models per se.

title: No procedure defines clinically defensible equivalence classes of treatment versions
text: STR-01 Unverifiable High priority Emerging Tractability 3/5

title: No procedure defines clinically defensible equivalence classes of treatment versions
text:
Statement
Estimating a per-protocol effect requires the sustained strategy and its relevant treatment versions to be clinically specified first; artificial censoring with inverse probability weighting is one valid estimation route rather than a requirement. Beneath the mechanics sits the question the mechanics assume answered: what counts as the same treatment. Real treatments differ by dose, route, provider, formulation, combination and adherence pattern, and two regimens sharing a label may not satisfy consistency. Clone-censor-weight handles a patient compatible with several predefined strategies and does not decide whether versions should be pooled into one. Observed data can expose heterogeneity across versions and cannot establish that versions are irrelevant, so the pooling decision is clinical. Finer definitions also create practical support problems, so the more faithful specification is often the less identifiable one, and no guidance exists for making that trade.

title: No procedure defines clinically defensible equivalence classes of treatment versions
text:
Why it is open
Consistency is an assumption about the world rather than about the data, so no amount of data adjudicates whether two versions are the same treatment; heterogeneity across versions is evidence against pooling and its absence is not evidence for it. The clinical judgment that would adjudicate is specific to the drug, the indication and the era, which makes a general criterion the wrong shape. And making the versions explicit multiplies the strategies, each costing positivity, so the honest specification is frequently the one the data cannot support.

title: No procedure defines clinically defensible equivalence classes of treatment versions
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Gaber CE, Ghazarian AA, Strassle PD, et al. De-mystifying the clone-censor-weight method for causal research using observational data. Cancer Med 2024
A didactic account of cloning, artificial censoring and censoring weights, including the computational cost and the sensitivity to the censoring model.


Cain LE, Robins JM, Lanoy E, Logan R, Costagliola D, Hernán MA. Using observational data to emulate a randomized trial of dynamic treatment-switching strategies. Int J Epidemiol 2016;45(6):2038-2049
Defines dynamic switching strategies precisely enough to emulate, which is the closest existing template for specifying what a strategy includes.


lmtp: Non-Parametric Causal Effects of Feasible Interventions Based on Modified Treatment Policies. CRAN
Supports continuous and multivariate treatments, which is the representation a dose-and-adherence strategy needs.

title: No procedure defines clinically defensible equivalence classes of treatment versions
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Use hierarchical treatment ontologies and latent treatment-version models so the equivalence class is an explicit, versioned object, and report the observed heterogeneity across versions as evidence bearing on the pooling decision rather than as a robustness check. Estimate joint effects of initiation, dose and adherence through longitudinal multivariate modified treatment policies where an analyst-specified joint policy is what is wanted, noting that such an estimator does not supply the equivalence classes and need not target the same per-protocol estimand. Quantify by simulation how much bias a wrong equivalence class induces relative to the positivity cost of the correct one, since that trade is the actual decision.

title: No procedure defines clinically defensible equivalence classes of treatment versions
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source said. “A per-protocol effect requires censoring at deviation and weighting for the informative censoring that censoring creates. Beneath that mechanics sits a question the mechanics assume away: what counts as the same treatment. Real treatments differ by dose, route, provider, formulation, combination and adherence pattern, and two regimens sharing a label may not satisfy consistency. Clone-censor-weight handles the case where baseline assignment is genuinely ambiguous, at the cost of data expansion, artificial censoring and sensitivity to the censoring model, but it takes the strategy definition as given. There is no guidance for constructing defensible equivalence classes of treatment versions, and none for overlapping combination therapies where a patient is simultaneously compatible with more than one labeled strategy.”
What was wrong with it. Three corrections. Artificial censoring with inverse probability weighting is one valid way to estimate a per-protocol effect, not a requirement. Clone-censor-weight does handle individuals compatible with several predefined strategies, which the entry listed as unaddressed; what it does not do is decide whether treatment versions should be pooled. And observed data can expose heterogeneity across versions even though they cannot establish that versions are irrelevant, so the situation is not entirely uninformative.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported-with-caveat): The treatment-versions problem has a longer literature than the entry credits. Confounding adjustment in the presence of multiple versions of treatment was worked out for an organ-transplant application in 2019, and marginal structural models for partial exposure regimes date to 2008. A 2026 iScience paper shows that changing the exposure definition unmasks confounding in an applied emulation, which is empirical evidence for the entry’s premise and also evidence that the field is examining it. What remains genuinely absent is guidance for constructing defensible equivalence classes and for overlapping combination therapies, which is the constructive half of the entry rather than the diagnostic half. codex dissented (overstated): Treatment-version ambiguity is real: collapsing causally different doses, formulations, routes, combinations, or adherence patterns can make the named intervention ill-defined. However, the report overstates both the required mechanics and the remaining gap. Estimating a per-protocol effect does not require artificial censoring plus inverse-probability weighting; the longitudinal g-formula and targeted or sequential-regression estimators can estimate sustained-strategy effects under their respective identification and modeling conditions. Clone-censor-weight already provides the bookkeeping for individuals compatible with multiple prespecified strategies, although it cannot choose those strategies or determine which versions are equivalent. Observed data cannot prove treatment-version irrelevance, but version-specific data can reveal heterogeneity and inform clinical judgment. Finer definitions may worsen practical support and precision, but every additional strategy does not mechanically violate positivity. Pinned lmtp 1.5.4 is correctly described: its NAMESPACE exports lmtp_tmle and lmtp_sdr, while its source accepts list-valued treatment nodes and applies analyst-specified multivariate shifts. It therefore supports estimation after a joint policy has been defined, not construction of clinical equivalence classes. Moreover, a longitudinal modified treatment policy generally targets a natural-value-dependent policy estimand, not automatically the per-protocol effect of a fixed sustained strategy. The issue is decision-critical when collapsed versions have materially different effects; a universal treatment ontology or latent-version model is a roadmap item rather than a prerequisite for every well-specified emulation.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. Inverted-prior search does not find a procedure that constructs clinically defensible equivalence classes of treatment versions for consistency in sustained-strategy target-trial emulation. The report’s own cited works do not close the gap: Gaber et al. (2024, 10.1002/cam4.70461) is a didactic CCW primer that takes the strategy as given; Cain et al. (2016, 10.1093/ije/dyv295) is the closest specification template for dynamic switching but does not adjudicate dose, route, formulation, provider, or combination-version equivalence; lmtp supplies estimation for continuous and multivariate modified treatment policies once an intervention is defined, not a clinical rule for which versions may be labeled the same treatment. Classic prior art formalizes the identification problem without solving clinical construction: VanderWeele and Hernán (2013, J Causal Inference; multiple versions) and Hernán and VanderWeele (2011, compound treatments) show when version-mixed averages versus version-specific effects are identifiable, which strengthens rather than resolves the claim that consistency is a world assumption adjudicated by clinical judgment specific to drug, indication, and era. 2024–2026 work remains proposal-level or off-scope. Yoshikawa and Kawano (arXiv:2601.00287, 2026) propose mixture-of-experts estimation of latent versions under point treatment; the number of versions is pre-specified, versions are data-driven latent classes rather than clinically specified equivalence classes, and the paper itself notes that version-specific methodology was previously underdeveloped. That is a partial advance along the report’s proposed latent-version direction, not a solved clinical procedure, and it does not cover sustained or dynamic strategies or overlapping multi-drug regimens. Ostropolets et al. (2024) ATC–RxNorm hierarchies improve drug coding and retrieval; they are not causal equivalence classes for consistency. Fu et al. (BMJ 2026) and related CCW guidance clarify cloning when baseline data are compatible with more than one labeled strategy; that is the mechanics the report already credits, still leaving strategy definition as input. Practical TTE guides (e.g. Fridén 2026) restate “define interventions so relevant multiple versions do not exist” without a constructive algorithm. Package release notes and GitHub activity for TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, gfoRmulaICE, lmtp, ltmle, WeightIt, MatchIt, and related tools implement estimation given a user-defined regimen; none encode an equivalence-class constructor. 2025–2026 FDA RWE / externally controlled trial materials, EMA/HMA registry guidance, HARPER/STaRT-RWE, ENCePP, and TARGET-style reporting require explicit treatment-strategy specification but do not supply a general method for building clinically defensible version sets or for adjudicating simultaneous multi-strategy compatibility beyond cloning. Because consistency is structurally untestable from data alone, sensitivity analyses and latent-mixture recoveries quantify consequences or statistical heterogeneity; they do not identify clinical sameness. Queries that returned nothing closing the gap included combinations of: treatment version equivalence class + target trial; clinically defensible versions of treatment + consistency; hierarchical ontology + causal strategy definition + sustained treatment; overlapping combination therapy + clone-censor equivalence; and journal-restricted 2024–2026 searches in AJE, Epidemiology, IJE, Stat Med, Biometrics, BMJ, JAMA, plus arXiv stat.ME and medRxiv. Residual risk is a narrowly scoped clinical protocol for one drug class that was not indexed under causal-inference terms; that would at most partially narrow the problem for that class, not the general gap as stated.

glm

abstain / supported-with-caveat. The claim is internally consistent and identifies a genuine structural tension: consistency is an assumption about the world, not the data, so clinical adjudication of treatment-version equivalence is inherently context-specific (drug, indication, era). The report’s own reasoning—that ‘a general criterion [is] the wrong shape for the problem’—supports a structural impossibility for a universal procedure, which is a stronger and more defensible claim than the empirical assertion that ‘no guidance exists.’ The latter is a negative existential about the current literature that I cannot verify without search. Additionally, the report itself cites Cain et al. 2016 as ‘the closest existing template for specifying what a strategy includes,’ which suggests related guidance exists even if it does not directly address equivalence-class construction. The claim is pitched at a level that conflates a structural limitation (no general procedure can work) with an empirical gap (no guidance has been written), and the proposed direction (ontologies, latent models, modified treatment policies) implies that partial frameworks are possible, undercutting the implication that the problem is permanently intractable. The severity is proportionate: a wrong equivalence class induces bias, and the positivity trade-off is a real decision cost. I abstain on status because confirming the absence of all guidance requires literature search I cannot perform.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2/3) → R7:counter-and-support-both-present(support=1/counter=1)
